subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define psychology.
answer_html:
Definition Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes of human beings (and animals).

Points to remember

  1. The word comes from the Greek psyche (soul, mind) and logos (study)
  2. It was first called the "science of the soul", then of the "mind", then of "consciousness"; today it is the science of behaviour
  3. Woodworth: psychology is the scientific study of the activities of the individual in relation to his environment
  4. Wilhelm Wundt set up the first psychology laboratory at Leipzig in 1879 – the beginning of scientific psychology
  5. "Behaviour" includes observable actions; "mental processes" include thinking, feeling, perceiving, remembering

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Name the methods of psychology.
answer_html:
Introduction Psychologists use scientific methods to study behaviour.

Methods

  1. Introspection – looking inward and reporting one's own experiences
  2. Observation – watching behaviour in natural settings
  3. Experimental method – controlled study of cause and effect
  4. Case study (case history) – in-depth study of one person
  5. Survey and questionnaire – collecting information from many people
  6. Interview – face-to-face questioning
  7. Psychological tests – standardised measurement of abilities and traits
  8. Developmental methods – longitudinal and cross-sectional studies
  9. Clinical method – study and treatment of individuals with problems

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the branches of pure psychology.
answer_html:
Introduction Psychology has two main divisions:

  • Pure psychology – develops theories and principles of behaviour; aims at knowledge
  • Applied psychology – uses these principles to solve practical problems (clinical, counselling, educational, industrial, health psychology)

Branches of pure psychology

1. General psychology

  • Studies the basic principles of normal adult behaviour – sensation, perception, learning, memory, thinking, motivation, emotion, intelligence, personality
  • Forms the foundation for all other branches

2. Abnormal psychology

  • Studies abnormal behaviour and mental disorders – their causes, symptoms and classification
  • The base of psychiatry and psychiatric nursing

3. Developmental (child) psychology

  • Studies growth and changes in behaviour across the life span – infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood and old age

4. Social psychology

  • Studies how individuals think, feel and behave in groups – attitudes, prejudice, leadership, conformity, group behaviour

5. Experimental psychology

  • Studies behaviour through controlled laboratory experiments – e.g. memory, learning, reaction time

6. Physiological (biological) psychology

  • Studies the relationship between body functions and behaviour – role of the brain, nervous system, hormones and genes

7. Psychology of personality

  • Studies the structure, development and assessment of personality and individual differences

8. Cognitive psychology

  • Studies mental processes – attention, perception, memory, language, problem solving

9. Comparative (animal) psychology

  • Compares the behaviour of animals and humans

10. Para-psychology

  • Studies unusual experiences such as telepathy and extrasensory perception (not well accepted scientifically)

Applied branches (for comparison): clinical, counselling, educational, health, industrial (organisational), forensic and community psychology.

Pure vs applied psychology

Point Pure psychology Applied psychology
Aim builds knowledge, theories and laws solves practical problems
Setting laboratories, research centres hospitals, schools, industries, courts
Example studying how memory works helping a student who forgets easily
Outcome principles of behaviour services – therapy, counselling, guidance

Importance for nurses

  • General psychology – knowledge of learning, memory and motivation helps in patient teaching
  • Developmental psychology – care of children, adolescents and the elderly according to their stage of life
  • Social psychology – understanding attitudes, group behaviour and teamwork in the ward and community
  • Abnormal psychology – recognising early signs of mental illness and referring in time
  • Physiological psychology – understanding how illness, hormones and drugs change behaviour

Conclusion Pure psychology includes general, abnormal, developmental, social, experimental, physiological, personality and cognitive psychology; it provides the principles that applied psychology and nursing use in practice.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the significance of psychology in nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Nursing is concerned with the whole person – body, mind and social life. Illness affects a patient's feelings, thinking and behaviour, and these in turn affect recovery. Knowledge of psychology helps the nurse understand and care for the patient as a human being, and also helps the nurse understand herself.

1. Understanding the patient's behaviour

  • Patients may show fear, anxiety, anger, denial, dependency or depression
  • Psychology explains these reactions so the nurse responds with patience and empathy instead of irritation

2. Holistic nursing care

  • Meeting psychological needs – security, belonging, self-esteem – along with physical needs
  • Recognising the mind–body relationship (stress worsens hypertension, asthma, peptic ulcer)

3. Effective communication and interpersonal relationship

  • Therapeutic communication, active listening and empathy build trust
  • Good nurse–patient relationship improves cooperation and satisfaction

4. Care of patients of different ages

  • Developmental psychology helps in caring for children, adolescents, adults and the elderly according to their needs

5. Mental health promotion

  • Recognising early warning signs of mental illness
  • Counselling, stress management and crisis support

6. Patient education

  • Principles of learning, memory and motivation help nurses teach patients effectively and improve compliance

7. Care of special groups

  • Dying patients, disabled persons, victims of abuse, chronically ill patients

8. Self-understanding and professional growth

  • Understanding one's own emotions, attitudes and stress
  • Managing work stress and preventing burnout
  • Developing personality, soft skills and leadership

9. Teamwork and management

  • Group behaviour, motivation and leadership help in working with the health team and managing a ward

10. Research

  • Psychological methods and tests are used in nursing research

11. Support to the patient's family

  • Relatives are anxious too; understanding their fear helps the nurse give clear information and involve them in care
  • Families of chronically ill, dying or mentally ill patients need emotional support and guidance

12. Handling difficult situations

  • Angry, demanding, uncooperative or confused patients are handled calmly when the nurse understands the cause of the behaviour
  • Breaking bad news, caring for a patient after a suicide attempt and supporting the bereaved need psychological skills

Ward example A 9-year-old boy admitted for appendicectomy cries, refuses injections and asks for his mother. A nurse who knows child psychology lets the mother stay, explains the procedure in simple words, praises him for cooperating and keeps his favourite toy nearby. The child settles, cooperates and recovers faster.

Conclusion Psychology helps the nurse understand patients' behaviour and needs, communicate effectively, promote mental health, teach patients and manage her own stress – making nursing care holistic and humane.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define psychology. Describe the methods of psychology. (2 + 8)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes
  • Derived from the Greek psyche (soul, mind) and logos (study)
  • Woodworth: "Psychology is the scientific study of the activities of the individual in relation to his environment"
  • Modern psychology began when Wilhelm Wundt established the first psychology laboratory in Leipzig in 1879
  • Its goals are to describe, explain, predict and control (modify) behaviour

(b) Methods of psychology (8 marks) Psychology uses scientific methods to collect facts about behaviour. The main methods are:

1. Introspection (self-observation)

  • The person looks inward and describes his own thoughts, feelings and experiences
  • Used by Wundt and the structuralists
  • Merits: the only way to know one's inner experiences directly; simple; needs no equipment
  • Limitations: subjective; cannot be checked by others; not possible with children, animals or the mentally ill; the act of observing changes the feeling

2. Observation method

  • Systematic watching and recording of behaviour as it occurs
  • Types:
    • Naturalistic – in the natural setting (children at play)
    • Participant – the observer becomes part of the group
    • Controlled – in a planned situation
  • Merits: objective; useful for children, animals and patients; studies real-life behaviour
  • Limitations: observer bias; behaviour may change when people know they are watched; time-consuming; cannot show cause and effect
  • In nursing: observation of patients' behaviour, pain and mood is a daily nursing skill

3. Experimental method – the most scientific method

  • Studies cause-and-effect relationships under controlled conditions
  • Independent variable – the factor changed by the experimenter (e.g. hours of sleep)
  • Dependent variable – the behaviour measured (e.g. memory score)
  • Experimental group receives the treatment; control group does not
  • Merits: precise, objective, can be repeated; shows causes
  • Limitations: artificial situations; many human problems cannot be studied experimentally for ethical reasons
  • Steps: identify the problem → form a hypothesis → select subjects and divide them into experimental and control groups → keep other variables constant → apply the independent variable → measure the dependent variable → analyse results → draw conclusions
  • Example: to test whether soft music reduces pre-operative anxiety, one group of patients listens to music before surgery and another does not; the anxiety scores of the two groups are then compared

4. Case study (case history) method

  • Detailed study of one individual (or family) – history, background, development, problems
  • Information from interviews, records, tests and observation
  • Merits: in-depth understanding; useful in clinical psychology and psychiatric nursing
  • Limitations: results cannot be generalised; depends on memory of informants
  • Steps: identify the problem → collect history (personal, family, developmental, medical, social) → examination and tests → diagnosis → plan of treatment → follow-up
  • In nursing: case studies are part of nursing education and help in planning individualised care

5. Survey and questionnaire method

  • Collecting information from a large number of people through printed questions or forms
  • Merits: quick, economical, reaches many people
  • Limitations: honesty of responses; limited to literate respondents (if self-administered)

6. Interview method

  • Face-to-face conversation to collect information
  • Structured (fixed questions) or unstructured (free conversation)
  • Merits: flexible; can be used with illiterate people; observation of non-verbal cues
  • Limitations: interviewer bias; time-consuming

7. Psychological tests

  • Standardised instruments to measure intelligence, aptitude, personality, attitudes and interests
  • Merits: objective, comparable with norms
  • Limitations: need trained testers; cultural bias

8. Developmental methods

  • Longitudinal method – the same group is studied over many years
  • Cross-sectional method – different age groups are studied at one time

9. Clinical method

  • Used to study and treat individuals with psychological problems, combining interviews, case history, tests and observation

10. Correlational method

  • Finds the relationship between two variables (e.g. stress and blood pressure), but does not prove cause

Comparison of main methods

Method Strength Weakness
Introspection direct inner experience subjective
Observation real-life behaviour observer bias
Experiment shows cause and effect artificial
Case study in-depth not generalisable
Survey covers many people honesty of answers

Characteristics of a good (scientific) method

  • Objective – free from personal bias of the observer
  • Reliable – gives the same results when repeated
  • Valid – measures what it claims to measure
  • Systematic – planned steps, careful recording
  • Verifiable – other workers can check the findings
  • Ethical – informed consent, privacy and confidentiality, no harm to subjects

Use in nursing

  • Observation – of pain, mood, sleep, behaviour and response to treatment, recorded in nurses' notes
  • Interview – nursing history on admission, counselling sessions
  • Case study – case presentations and individualised care plans
  • Rating scales and tests – pain scales, Glasgow Coma Scale, anxiety and depression scales
  • Experiments and surveys – in nursing research projects

Conclusion Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. It uses introspection, observation, experiments, case studies, surveys, interviews and tests – each with its own merits and limitations – and nurses use many of these methods in everyday patient assessment.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Name the schools of psychology with their founders.
answer_html:
Introduction Schools of psychology are the different viewpoints from which psychologists have studied behaviour and the mind.

  1. Structuralism – Wilhelm Wundt (first psychology laboratory, Leipzig, 1879) and Titchener; studied the structure of the conscious mind by introspection
  2. Functionalism – William James; studied how the mind helps us adapt to the environment
  3. Behaviourism – J. B. Watson, later B. F. Skinner; studied only observable behaviour and learning
  4. Gestalt psychology – Wertheimer, Köhler, Koffka; "the whole is more than the sum of its parts" – perception and insight
  5. Psychoanalysis – Sigmund Freud; the unconscious mind, id–ego–superego, defence mechanisms
  6. Humanistic psychology – Abraham Maslow, Carl Rogers; free will, growth and self-actualisation
  7. Cognitive psychology – Neisser, Piaget; mental processes such as memory, thinking and problem solving

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define behaviour. Give its types.
answer_html:
Definition Behaviour is any activity of a person that can be observed or measured, including actions, speech, thoughts and feelings, in response to stimuli from the environment. Kurt Lewin expressed it as B = f(P, E) – behaviour is a function of the person and the environment.

Types

  1. Overt (external) – can be seen by others: walking, talking, crying
  2. Covert (internal) – cannot be seen: thinking, feeling, remembering, dreaming
  3. Voluntary (deliberate) and involuntary (reflex, e.g. blinking)
  4. Conscious and unconscious
  5. Simple (reflex) and complex (learned skills)
  6. Normal (adaptive) and abnormal (maladaptive)

Nursing importance: nurses observe and record behaviour accurately – it reflects the patient's physical and mental state.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the relationship of psychology with other subjects.
answer_html:
Introduction Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. Because human behaviour is affected by the body, society and culture, psychology is closely related to many other subjects; each borrows from and contributes to the others.

1. Psychology and biology (physiology)

  • Behaviour depends on the brain, nerves and hormones
  • Physiological (biological) psychology studies these links – e.g. thyroid disorders change mood; brain injury changes personality

2. Psychology and sociology

  • Psychology studies the individual; sociology studies groups and society
  • Social psychology bridges them – attitudes, prejudice, leadership, group behaviour and socialisation

3. Psychology and anthropology

  • Anthropology studies culture; psychology studies how culture shapes personality and behaviour (cross-cultural psychology)

4. Psychology and education

  • Educational psychology applies principles of learning, motivation, memory and individual differences to teaching, guidance and evaluation

5. Psychology and medicine

  • Psychosomatic disorders show the link between mind and body
  • Health psychology studies stress, illness behaviour, pain and compliance
  • Psychiatry (a branch of medicine) treats mental disorders, while clinical psychology assesses them and provides psychotherapy

6. Psychology and nursing

  • Helps the nurse understand patients' needs, emotions and behaviour
  • Basis of therapeutic communication, patient teaching and stress management

7. Psychology and philosophy

  • Psychology began as a part of philosophy (the mind–body question); it became an independent science in 1879

8. Psychology and other fields

  • Economics and management – consumer behaviour, work motivation (industrial psychology)
  • Law – forensic psychology, criminal behaviour, eyewitness testimony
  • Statistics – psychological testing and research (psychometrics)

Summary table

Subject Link with psychology
Physiology brain, hormones and behaviour
Sociology individual in the group – social psychology
Education learning and teaching
Medicine psychosomatic illness, health psychology
Nursing patient behaviour, communication, emotional care

Psychology and psychiatry compared

Psychology Psychiatry
science of normal and abnormal behaviour branch of medicine dealing with mental disorders
psychologist – trained in psychology psychiatrist – a medical doctor
uses tests, counselling and psychotherapy diagnoses, prescribes medicines and other treatments

Why these links matter to the nurse

  • The nurse works in a team with doctors, psychologists, social workers and teachers; knowing these links helps her coordinate holistic care

Conclusion Psychology is linked with physiology, sociology, anthropology, education, medicine, nursing, philosophy, law and economics; these links help the nurse understand the patient as a whole person.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the body–mind relationship.
answer_html:
Introduction Body and mind are not separate; they constantly influence each other. This is called the body–mind (psychosomatic) relationship.

1. Mind affects body

  • Stress and anxiety → raised BP, palpitations, sweating, peptic ulcer, worsening of asthma and diabetes
  • Fear before surgery → rapid pulse, loss of appetite
  • Hope and confidence speed recovery (placebo effect)

2. Body affects mind

  • Pain, fever and chronic illness → irritability, depression
  • Hormonal changes (thyroid, menstrual cycle) alter mood
  • Hunger, fatigue, drugs and alcohol change behaviour and thinking

Nursing importance: give holistic care – relieve physical discomfort and also reduce fear and anxiety.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Outline the process of sensation.
answer_html:
Definition Sensation is the process by which our sense organs receive stimuli from the environment and the body and send them to the brain, producing a simple awareness (e.g. seeing light, hearing sound).

Process of sensation

  1. Stimulus – light, sound, heat, pressure or a chemical
  2. Receptor – a sense organ (eye, ear, skin, tongue, nose) receives the stimulus
  3. Transduction – the receptor converts the stimulus into a nerve impulse
  4. Conduction – the impulse travels along the sensory nerve
  5. Brain – reaches the sensory area of the cerebral cortex
  6. Sensation – the person becomes aware of the stimulus; when it is interpreted, it becomes perception

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the role of heredity and environment in behaviour.
answer_html:
Introduction Every individual is the product of heredity and environment. Heredity provides the potential; environment decides how far this potential develops. Neither acts alone – they interact continuously.

A. Heredity 1. Meaning: the transmission of physical and mental traits from parents to children through genes.

  • Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46); half come from each parent
  • Genes on chromosomes carry the genetic code (DNA)

2. Traits influenced by heredity

  • Physical features – height, colour of skin, eyes and hair, blood group
  • Intelligence potential and special abilities (music, art)
  • Temperament – activity level, emotional reactivity
  • Predisposition to illnesses – schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, depression, alcoholism, diabetes, hypertension
  • Genetic disorders – Down syndrome (trisomy 21), phenylketonuria (intellectual disability if untreated), thalassaemia

3. Evidence: twin studies – identical twins are more alike in intelligence and personality than fraternal twins, even when reared apart.

B. Environment 1. Meaning: all the external influences acting on a person from conception to death.

2. Types

  • Prenatal environment – maternal nutrition, infections (rubella), drugs, alcohol, smoking, radiation, stress
  • Physical environment – climate, housing, pollution
  • Social environment – family, parenting style, school, peers, culture, religion, socio-economic status, mass media
  • Nutritional – iodine and iron deficiency affect brain development

3. Behaviour shaped by environment: language, habits, values, attitudes, skills, interests and much of personality.

Heredity vs environment at a glance

Point Heredity Environment
Source genes from both parents surroundings from conception onwards
Time of action fixed at conception acts throughout life
What it gives potential and limits opportunity and direction
Can it be changed? no (only counselling before conception) yes – by nutrition, care, education

C. Interaction of heredity and environment

  • Heredity sets the limits (range); environment decides where within this range a person develops
  • A child with good intellectual potential may not develop it if poorly nourished and unstimulated
  • A child with a family history of mental illness may stay well in a supportive, low-stress environment

D. Nursing importance

  • Genetic counselling, avoidance of consanguineous marriage
  • Good antenatal care, nutrition and avoidance of harmful substances in pregnancy
  • Early stimulation and supportive parenting
  • Recognising family history in mental and physical illnesses

Conclusion Heredity gives the raw material and environment moulds it; behaviour is the result of their constant interaction, so nurses work on improving the environment to help each person reach full potential.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the relationship between the brain and behaviour.
answer_html:
Introduction All behaviour – thinking, feeling, remembering and acting – depends on the brain and nervous system, together with the endocrine glands. Damage or chemical changes in the brain therefore change behaviour.

1. Cerebral cortex

  • Frontal lobe – personality, judgement, planning, self-control, voluntary movement, speech (Broca's area); damage → personality change, poor judgement
  • Parietal lobe – body sensation, awareness of body and space
  • Temporal lobe – hearing, understanding language (Wernicke's area), memory
  • Occipital lobe – vision

2. Limbic system – the "emotional brain"

  • Amygdala – fear, anger, aggression
  • Hippocampus – forming new memories (damaged early in Alzheimer's disease)

3. Hypothalamus

  • Controls hunger, thirst, sleep, sex drive, body temperature and aggression
  • Controls the pituitary and the autonomic nervous system – link between mind and body in stress

4. Reticular activating system (brainstem)

  • Controls arousal, alertness, attention and the sleep–wake cycle

5. Cerebellum – coordination, balance, motor learning.

6. Neurotransmitters (chemical messengers)

  • Dopamine – reward, pleasure, movement; excess linked with schizophrenia, deficiency with Parkinson's disease
  • Serotonin – mood, sleep, appetite; low levels linked with depression
  • Noradrenaline – alertness, arousal; anxiety and stress
  • GABA – calming, inhibitory (anti-anxiety drugs act here)
  • Acetylcholine – memory, learning (reduced in Alzheimer's disease)

7. Endocrine glands and behaviour

  • Thyroid – hypothyroidism causes slowness and depression; hyperthyroidism causes anxiety, irritability and restlessness
  • Adrenal glands – adrenaline and cortisol in stress and emotions
  • Sex hormones – behaviour changes at puberty; mood changes before periods and after delivery
  • Pancreas – hypoglycaemia causes confusion and abnormal behaviour

8. Effects of brain disorders on behaviour

  • Stroke – paralysis, speech problems (aphasia), emotional changes and depression
  • Frontal lobe injury – loss of self-control, rude or careless behaviour, poor judgement
  • Alzheimer's disease – loss of recent memory, confusion, wandering, personality change
  • Epilepsy – episodes of altered consciousness and behaviour
  • Brain infections and tumours – confusion, irritability, change in personality

9. Nursing importance

  • Behaviour changes after head injury, stroke, brain tumour or dementia have physical causes – patients need patience and safety
  • Many psychiatric drugs act on neurotransmitters – observe effects and side effects
  • Check blood sugar and thyroid status in confused or anxious patients

Conclusion The brain, its chemical messengers and the endocrine glands form the biological basis of behaviour; changes in any of them change how a person thinks, feels and acts.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define sensation. Explain the attributes of sensation and the abnormalities of sensory processes with nursing implications. (2 + 4 + 4)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Sensation is the process of receiving information (stimuli) from the environment and from within the body through the sense organs and conveying it to the brain
  • It is the first step in knowing the world; when the brain interprets a sensation and gives it meaning, it becomes perception
  • Senses: vision, hearing, smell, taste, touch (skin senses – touch, pressure, pain, heat, cold), and internal senses – kinaesthetic (position and movement), vestibular (balance) and organic (hunger, thirst, pain from organs)

Process: stimulus → receptor → transduction into nerve impulse → sensory nerve → sensory area of the brain → sensation.

Senses and their receptors

Sense Receptor Stimulus
Vision rods and cones of the retina light
Hearing organ of Corti in the cochlea sound waves
Smell olfactory cells in the nose chemicals in the air
Taste taste buds of the tongue chemicals in solution
Skin senses receptors in the skin touch, pressure, heat, cold, pain
Kinaesthetic muscles, tendons and joints position and movement of body parts
Vestibular semicircular canals of inner ear balance, head movement
Organic internal organs hunger, thirst, nausea, visceral pain

Sensation vs perception

Sensation Perception
receiving the stimulus interpreting the stimulus
simple awareness ("a sound") meaningful experience ("the ward phone is ringing")
depends on sense organs depends also on past experience, attention, needs

(b) Attributes (characteristics) of sensation (4 marks)

  1. Quality – the kind of sensation (red or blue colour, sweet or bitter taste)
  2. Intensity – the strength (bright or dim light, loud or soft sound)
  3. Duration – how long the sensation lasts
  4. Extensity – how large an area it covers (a pinprick vs pressure of a palm)
  5. Local sign – the ability to tell where on the body the sensation is coming from

Thresholds

  • Absolute threshold – the minimum intensity of a stimulus that can be detected
  • Difference threshold – the smallest difference between two stimuli that can be noticed (Weber's law)

Sensory adaptation

  • Decrease in sensitivity to a constant stimulus – we stop noticing the smell of a ward or the touch of our clothes after a while

(c) Abnormalities of sensory processes and nursing implications (4 marks)

1. Sensory deprivation

  • Too little meaningful stimulation – in isolation wards, ICU, prolonged bed rest, blindness, deafness, elderly living alone, patients with eye patches
  • Effects: boredom, restlessness, anxiety, disorientation, confusion, illusions, even hallucinations; slowed thinking; depression
  • Nursing: orient the patient to time, place and person; clock and calendar; talk to the patient during care; encourage visitors; radio, newspapers; allow personal belongings; spectacles and hearing aids in place

2. Sensory overload

  • Too much stimulation at once – noise, bright lights, alarms, constant procedures in ICU, crowded wards, pain
  • Effects: irritability, anxiety, confusion, inability to concentrate, sleep disturbance ("ICU psychosis" or delirium)
  • Nursing: reduce noise and lights at night, cluster nursing activities, allow uninterrupted rest, explain sounds and procedures, limit visitors when needed

3. Sensory deficits

  • Impaired vision or hearing, loss of smell or taste, loss of sensation in diabetes (neuropathy) or leprosy
  • Effects: risk of injury (falls, burns, pressure ulcers), social isolation, poor appetite
  • Nursing: safety measures (side rails, lighting, checking bath water temperature), foot care in diabetics, communication aids, facing deaf patients while speaking

4. Other abnormal sensations

  • Anaesthesia (loss of sensation), hypoaesthesia (reduced), hyperaesthesia (increased), paraesthesia (tingling, pins and needles), phantom limb sensation
  • Illusions (misinterpretation of a real stimulus) and hallucinations (perception without a stimulus) – may occur in delirium, sensory deprivation and mental illness

5. Sensory changes in special groups

  • Elderly – presbyopia (difficulty in near vision), cataract, presbycusis (hearing loss for high tones), reduced taste, smell and pain sensation → risk of falls, burns, poor appetite and isolation
  • Newborns and infants – senses are developing; they need gentle touch, the mother's voice and warmth
  • Unconscious patients – hearing may be the last sense to be lost, so the nurse talks to them and explains every procedure

General nursing principles

  • Assess sensory function on admission – vision (reading a newspaper), hearing (whisper test), touch and pain sensation, smell and taste – and record any deficit in the care plan
  • Provide meaningful but not excessive stimulation
  • Ensure safety and maintain orientation to time, place and person
  • Use touch therapeutically and appropriately, respecting culture and gender
  • Teach families how to communicate with patients who have sensory losses
  • Arrange aids – spectacles, hearing aids, magnifiers, large-print labels on medicines

Conclusion Sensation is the first step of knowing the world, with attributes of quality, intensity, duration, extensity and local sign. Too little, too much or impaired sensory input disturbs behaviour, and nurses prevent this by providing a balanced, safe and orienting environment.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: List the characteristics of a mentally healthy person.
answer_html:
Introduction Mental health is a state of well-being in which a person realises his own abilities, can cope with the normal stresses of life, can work productively and contributes to his community (WHO).

Characteristics of a mentally healthy person

  1. Positive attitude towards self – self-acceptance, self-confidence
  2. Realistic perception of reality
  3. Emotional stability – controls emotions, does not get upset easily
  4. Copes with stress and frustration
  5. Good interpersonal relationships – gets along with others
  6. Adapts to change
  7. Works productively and takes responsibility
  8. Independence (autonomy) in decisions
  9. Realistic goals and a sense of purpose
  10. Sense of humour and enjoys life

subject: Applied Psychology
question: State the meaning of ego defence mechanism.
answer_html:
Definition Ego defence mechanisms are unconscious mental processes used by the ego to protect the person from anxiety, guilt and threats to self-esteem. The concept was given by Sigmund Freud and developed by Anna Freud.

Key points

  1. They work unconsciously (the person is not aware of using them)
  2. They distort or deny reality to some extent
  3. Everyone uses them; in moderation they are normal and help adjustment
  4. Excessive use is unhealthy and prevents solving the real problem

Examples: denial, repression, projection, rationalisation, regression, displacement, sublimation.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: List the warning signs of poor mental health.
answer_html:
Introduction Early recognition of warning signs allows timely help.

Warning signs

  1. Persistent sadness, hopelessness or crying spells
  2. Withdrawal from family, friends and activities
  3. Excessive worry, fear or anxiety
  4. Marked changes in sleep or appetite
  5. Extreme mood swings, irritability, anger outbursts
  6. Fall in performance at school or work; poor concentration
  7. Use of alcohol or drugs to cope
  8. Neglect of personal hygiene
  9. Unusual beliefs, suspiciousness, hearing voices
  10. Talk about death or suicide – needs urgent help

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Describe the promotive mental health strategies.
answer_html:
Introduction Mental health promotion means activities that strengthen mental well-being and help people cope with life, so that mental illness is less likely. It is different from treatment – it is meant for everyone, healthy or ill. Mental hygiene is the science of maintaining mental health and preventing mental disorders.

1. At the individual level

  • Healthy lifestyle – balanced diet, regular exercise, adequate sleep, avoiding tobacco, alcohol and drugs
  • Stress management – relaxation, deep breathing, yoga and meditation, hobbies
  • Life skills – problem-solving, decision-making, communication, coping with emotions
  • Positive thinking, self-esteem and realistic goals
  • Seeking help early when distressed

2. At the family level

  • Healthy child-rearing – love, security, consistent discipline, praise
  • Good communication and harmony in the family
  • Support during life transitions – marriage, childbirth, retirement, bereavement

3. At school and college

  • Life-skills education and school mental health programmes
  • Counselling services; anti-bullying measures
  • Adolescent health services (Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram)

4. At the workplace

  • Reasonable workload, supportive supervision, recognition
  • Stress management programmes, employee counselling, work–life balance

5. At the community level

  • Awareness programmes to reduce stigma about mental illness
  • Social support groups, self-help groups, recreational facilities
  • Programmes for vulnerable groups – elderly, disabled, migrants, disaster survivors
  • National Mental Health Programme and District Mental Health Programme
  • Tele-MANAS (14416) – free mental health helpline
  • Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 – rights of persons with mental illness

6. Preventive strategies (in brief)

  • Primary – prevent occurrence (good antenatal care, prevention of head injury, crisis intervention)
  • Secondary – early detection and treatment
  • Tertiary – rehabilitation and prevention of relapse

7. Mental health services

  • Psychiatric OPD and counselling in district hospitals; child guidance clinics
  • De-addiction centres; day-care and rehabilitation centres
  • Crisis helplines and tele-counselling (Tele-MANAS)

Role of the nurse

  • Health education on stress, sleep, substance use and warning signs of mental illness
  • Counselling and supportive talks for patients, students and families
  • Early identification of persons at risk – the elderly living alone, adolescents, new mothers, chronically ill – and timely referral
  • Reducing stigma by talking openly and respectfully about mental illness
  • Being a role model of a balanced, healthy lifestyle

Conclusion Promotive mental health strategies – healthy lifestyle, stress management, life skills, supportive families, schools and workplaces, and community awareness – help people stay mentally healthy and reduce the burden of mental illness.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain frustration and conflict and the ways to overcome them.
answer_html:
Introduction In daily life our goals are often blocked, or we must choose between competing goals. These situations produce frustration and conflict, which are major sources of stress.

A. Frustration 1. Definition: frustration is the feeling of disappointment, tension or anger that results when goal-directed behaviour is blocked.

2. Sources of frustration

  • Environmental – physical obstacles (traffic, illness), social barriers (rules, discrimination, poverty)
  • Personal – lack of ability, physical handicap, unrealistic goals, low self-confidence
  • Conflict between motives

3. Reactions: aggression, withdrawal, anxiety, regression, use of defence mechanisms, or constructive problem-solving.

B. Conflict 1. Definition: conflict is a state in which a person faces two or more incompatible motives or goals at the same time.

2. Types (Kurt Lewin)

  • Approach–approach – choosing between two attractive goals (two good job offers); easiest to resolve
  • Avoidance–avoidance – choosing between two unpleasant alternatives (painful surgery or continuing illness)
  • Approach–avoidance – one goal with both good and bad features (a well-paid job far from home); causes hesitation
  • Double (multiple) approach–avoidance – two or more goals, each with good and bad features; most difficult

C. Ways to overcome frustration and conflict

  1. Identify the real problem and analyse it calmly
  2. Problem-solving – gather information, consider alternatives, choose and act
  3. Set realistic goals according to one's abilities
  4. Change or substitute the goal when it is unattainable
  5. Develop skills and abilities to overcome obstacles
  6. Seek social support – talk to family, friends, teachers
  7. Relaxation, yoga, exercise and hobbies
  8. Healthy use of defence mechanisms – e.g. sublimation
  9. Counselling when distress persists

D. Role of the nurse in reducing frustration and conflict

  • Explain hospital routines and procedures to reduce uncertainty
  • Allow patients to participate in decisions about their care
  • Provide information to help patients choose between treatment options
  • Encourage expression of feelings; listen without judging
  • Meet needs promptly; avoid unnecessary restrictions
  • Help with problem-solving and refer to counsellors when needed

Conclusion Frustration arises when goals are blocked and conflict when goals compete; problem-solving, realistic goals, support and relaxation help people cope, and nurses can reduce both in patients through information, participation and emotional support.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define defence mechanisms. Explain the common defence mechanisms with examples and their implications for nursing. (2 + 6 + 2)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Defence mechanisms are unconscious mental processes used by the ego to protect the individual from anxiety, guilt and threats to self-esteem, by denying, distorting or disguising reality
  • The concept was introduced by Sigmund Freud and elaborated by his daughter Anna Freud
  • They arise from the conflict between the id (desires), the superego (conscience) and reality
  • Features: they are unconscious (except suppression), automatic, used by everyone, and helpful in moderation; overuse prevents real problem-solving and can lead to mental disorders

(b) Common defence mechanisms with examples (6 marks)

1. Repression

  • Unconsciously pushing painful thoughts or memories out of awareness
  • Example: a person cannot remember a traumatic accident
  • The basic defence on which others depend

2. Suppression

  • Consciously putting a worry out of mind for the time being
  • Example: a nurse puts aside her personal worries while on duty

3. Denial

  • Refusing to accept a painful reality
  • Example: a patient told he has cancer says, "The report must be wrong"; a common first reaction to bad news

4. Projection

  • Attributing one's own unacceptable thoughts or feelings to others
  • Example: a student who dislikes the teacher says, "The teacher hates me"

5. Rationalisation

  • Giving logical-sounding but false reasons to justify behaviour or failure
  • Example: "I failed because the questions were out of syllabus"; "sour grapes" thinking

6. Regression

  • Returning to an earlier stage of behaviour under stress
  • Example: a toilet-trained child starts bed-wetting or thumb-sucking when hospitalised or when a new baby arrives

7. Displacement

  • Transferring emotions from the real source to a safer target
  • Example: a patient angry about his illness shouts at the nurse; a man scolded by his boss shouts at his wife

8. Sublimation

  • Channelling unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable activities – the healthiest defence
  • Example: aggressive energy used in sports; a person who lost a child works for a children's charity

9. Reaction formation

  • Showing the opposite of one's true feelings
  • Example: being excessively polite to a person one dislikes

10. Compensation

  • Making up for a weakness by excelling in another area
  • Example: a student weak in sports works hard to top the class

11. Identification

  • Taking on the qualities of an admired person
  • Example: a nursing student imitating a respected senior nurse

12. Introjection

  • Taking in the values and attitudes of others as one's own (forms the conscience)

13. Intellectualisation

  • Using excessive reasoning to avoid emotions
  • Example: a patient discusses his heart attack in technical terms without showing fear

14. Conversion

  • Emotional conflict turned into physical symptoms without organic cause
  • Example: sudden "paralysis" of an arm after a severe emotional shock

15. Undoing

  • An act to cancel out an unacceptable thought or action
  • Example: buying gifts after quarrelling

16. Fantasy (day-dreaming)

  • Satisfying frustrated desires in imagination

Classification by level of maturity

Level Mechanisms Effect
Mature (healthy) sublimation, suppression, compensation, humour help adjustment and growth
Neurotic (intermediate) repression, displacement, reaction formation, rationalisation, intellectualisation, undoing relieve anxiety but hide the problem
Immature / psychotic denial of reality, projection, regression, fantasy (when extreme) distort reality; seen in severe stress and mental illness

Healthy vs unhealthy use

  • Healthy – used occasionally, for a short time, gives time to adjust, and the person still faces reality (temporary denial after hearing a diagnosis)
  • Unhealthy – used often, rigidly, for a long time, distorts reality and stops the person from solving the problem (a diabetic who keeps "forgetting" insulin because of denial)

Defence mechanisms commonly seen in the ward

Situation Mechanism
Patient refuses to believe his biopsy report denial
Hospitalised child wets the bed again regression
Patient angry about his illness shouts at the nurse displacement
Smoker says "my grandfather smoked and lived to 90" rationalisation
Patient with an amputated leg becomes a fine painter compensation / sublimation

(c) Implications for nursing (2 marks)

  • Recognise defence mechanisms in patients (denial of diagnosis, regression in children, displacement of anger onto staff) and respond with understanding, not argument or punishment
  • Allow temporary denial in the early stage of bad news; give information gradually as the patient is ready
  • Do not take a patient's anger personally – it is often displaced
  • Encourage healthy mechanisms such as sublimation and support patients to face problems realistically
  • When a mechanism is used excessively and interferes with treatment (e.g. persistent denial leading to refusal of treatment), refer for counselling
  • Nurses should also be aware of their own defences under stress

Conclusion Defence mechanisms are unconscious ways the ego protects us from anxiety. Used in moderation they help adjustment; used excessively they block problem-solving. Understanding them helps nurses respond to patients' behaviour with empathy.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the preventive strategies for mental health (levels of prevention).
answer_html:
Introduction Preventive mental health aims to prevent mental illness and its complications. Gerald Caplan described three levels of prevention.

A. Primary prevention – preventing the occurrence of mental illness Aim: to reduce new cases (incidence).

  • Health promotion – healthy lifestyle, nutrition, sleep, exercise, life-skills education in schools
  • Specific protection:
    • antenatal care; prevention of birth injury and infections (e.g. rubella)
    • iodised salt to prevent intellectual disability due to iodine deficiency
    • immunisation, genetic counselling, avoiding alcohol and drugs in pregnancy
  • Strong families – good parenting, prevention of child abuse and neglect
  • Coping skills and stress management; support during crises – bereavement, disasters (crisis intervention)
  • Reducing risk factors – poverty, unemployment, substance abuse; school and workplace mental health programmes

B. Secondary prevention – early diagnosis and prompt treatment Aim: to reduce the duration and severity of illness.

  • Screening of high-risk groups – students under stress, the elderly, mothers after delivery (postpartum depression), people with chronic illness
  • Early recognition of warning signs by teachers, nurses and community health workers
  • Crisis helplines – Tele-MANAS 14416
  • Prompt referral and treatment – District Mental Health Programme clinics, psychiatric units in general hospitals
  • Early treatment of substance use problems

C. Tertiary prevention – rehabilitation Aim: to reduce disability and prevent relapse.

  • Rehabilitation – vocational training, social skills training, day-care centres, half-way homes, sheltered workshops
  • Drug compliance and regular follow-up
  • Family psychoeducation – teaching families about the illness and reducing criticism and hostility at home
  • Reducing stigma and helping the person return to the community
  • Disability benefits – mental illness is a recognised disability

D. Role of the nurse

  • Primary – health education, life-skills sessions, antenatal care, support to families
  • Secondary – screening, early identification, referral, crisis support
  • Tertiary – medication supervision, rehabilitation, family support and follow-up

E. Examples of prevention in practice

Level Example Nurse's action
Primary life-skills sessions in a school teach coping and stress management
Secondary screening mothers for postpartum depression use a screening questionnaire; refer early
Tertiary a patient with schizophrenia returning home supervise medicines; family education; vocational referral

Conclusion Mental illness is prevented at three levels – primary (promotion and protection), secondary (early detection and treatment) and tertiary (rehabilitation and relapse prevention) – and the nurse is active at every level.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the factors affecting mental health.
answer_html:
Introduction Mental health is shaped by the interaction of biological, psychological and social factors (the biopsychosocial model). Some factors increase the risk of mental illness, while others protect mental health.

1. Biological factors

  • Heredity – family history of mental illness
  • Brain chemistry (neurotransmitters), brain injury and infections
  • Physical illness – thyroid disorders, chronic diseases, epilepsy, chronic pain
  • Nutrition – deficiency of iodine or vitamin B₁₂
  • Hormonal changes – puberty, pregnancy and after delivery, menopause
  • Alcohol and drugs; lack of sleep

2. Psychological factors

  • Early childhood experiences – love and security, or neglect and abuse
  • Personality – self-esteem and coping style
  • Emotional maturity; unresolved frustration and conflict
  • Stress and major life events – loss, failure, divorce

3. Family factors

  • Warm, supportive relationships protect; broken homes, domestic violence, overprotection or rejection harm
  • Parenting style and family communication

4. Social and economic factors

  • Social support and friendships – protective
  • Poverty, unemployment, debt and poor housing
  • Discrimination and stigma; social isolation and loneliness
  • Migration, urbanisation, disasters and violence
  • Culture and religion – can give meaning and support

5. Occupational and educational factors

  • Work stress, long hours, shift work, job insecurity, harassment
  • Academic pressure and examination stress

6. Lifestyle factors

  • Exercise, diet, sleep and leisure
  • Excessive screen time and social media use
  • Substance use

7. Life stage

  • Transitions – adolescence, marriage, retirement, old age

Protective factors at a glance

  • Good relationships and social support
  • Healthy lifestyle and physical health
  • Resilience and good coping skills
  • Meaningful work, hobbies and spiritual beliefs

Role of the nurse

  • Assess risk and protective factors during history-taking
  • Strengthen protective factors – family support, coping skills, healthy habits
  • Identify and refer people at risk

8. How the factors interact – an example

  • A student with a family history of depression (biological), facing examination stress (psychological), who has moved away from home and has few friends (social), is at much higher risk than a student with only one of these factors
  • Mental health problems usually result from several factors acting together

9. Role of the community and government

  • Mental health literacy and anti-stigma campaigns
  • Safe neighbourhoods, employment and social security schemes
  • Accessible mental health services – district programmes and telephone counselling

Conclusion Mental health depends on biological, psychological, family, social, occupational and lifestyle factors; reducing risk factors and strengthening protective ones keeps people mentally healthy.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Enumerate Piaget's stages of cognitive development.
answer_html:
Introduction Jean Piaget, a Swiss psychologist, explained how a child's thinking develops through four stages. Each stage builds on the previous one.

Stages

  1. Sensorimotor stage (birth – 2 years) – the baby learns through senses and movements; object permanence develops (knows a hidden toy still exists)
  2. Preoperational stage (2 – 7 years) – language and pretend play develop; thinking is egocentric (sees only his own point of view); believes objects are alive (animism); cannot understand conservation
  3. Concrete operational stage (7 – 11 years) – logical thinking about real, concrete things; understands conservation, classification and reversibility
  4. Formal operational stage (11 years onwards) – abstract and hypothetical thinking, scientific reasoning, planning for the future

subject: Applied Psychology
question: List the stages of dying according to Kubler-Ross.
answer_html:
Introduction Elisabeth Kubler-Ross (1969) described five emotional stages through which a dying person (and the family) usually passes. The stages may not come in order and may repeat.

Stages (memory aid: DABDA)

  1. Denial – "No, not me; the report must be wrong"
  2. Anger – "Why me?"; anger directed at family, doctors and nurses
  3. Bargaining – "If I live till my daughter's wedding, I will donate to the temple"
  4. Depression – sadness, crying, withdrawal as losses are realised
  5. Acceptance – calm, peaceful readiness for death

Nursing: accept the patient's reactions, listen, do not argue or give false hope, and support the family.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Differentiate between growth and development.
answer_html:
Introduction Growth and development go together but are not the same.

Growth Development
quantitative increase in size of the body or its parts qualitative, progressive change in function, skill and behaviour
measured in kg and cm (height, weight, head circumference) observed as milestones (sitting, walking, talking)
stops after adulthood continues throughout life
due to multiplication and enlargement of cells due to maturation and learning

Example: a child's weight increasing from 3 kg to 9 kg in one year is growth; learning to sit, stand and say "mama" is development.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the psychological needs of children and the role of the nurse in meeting them.
answer_html:
Introduction A child needs much more than food, clothing and medicine. For healthy development of personality, children have certain psychological (emotional and social) needs. Illness and hospitalisation – strange place, strange faces, pain and separation from parents – threaten these needs, so the nurse must consciously meet them.

Psychological needs of children

1. Love and affection

  • Every child needs to feel loved and wanted by parents and family
  • Lack of love leads to insecurity, poor self-esteem and behaviour problems

2. Security (safety)

  • Familiar persons, a predictable routine and protection from harm give a sense of safety
  • Separation from the mother in hospital causes separation anxiety – the child passes through protest (crying, clinging), despair (sad, withdrawn) and detachment (seems to lose interest in the parents)

3. Belonging and acceptance

  • The child needs to feel accepted as he is, whatever his looks, abilities or illness

4. Recognition, praise and approval

  • Praise for good behaviour builds self-esteem and encourages the child to repeat it

5. Independence (autonomy)

  • Toddlers and older children want to do things themselves – eat, dress, make small choices
  • Too much control causes shame, doubt and rebellion

6. Play and recreation

  • Play is the "work of the child"; it helps physical, mental, social and emotional development and relieves tension

7. New experiences and learning

  • Children are curious and need stimulation, questions answered and opportunities to explore

8. Discipline and guidance

  • Consistent, loving limits help the child learn right from wrong and feel secure

Role of the nurse in meeting these needs

  • Rooming-in: allow the mother or a close family member to stay with the child
  • Assign the same nurse as far as possible so the child can build trust
  • Prepare the child for procedures using simple words, dolls and pictures (therapeutic play); be honest when something will hurt
  • Allow a favourite toy, blanket or photo from home; follow home routines for feeding, sleeping and toileting
  • Never threaten a child with injections or punishment
  • Praise cooperation and bravery; give small rewards like stickers
  • Offer simple choices ("Which arm for the injection?") to support independence
  • Provide a play area, books and drawing materials; continue schoolwork during long stays
  • Respect the privacy of older children and adolescents
  • Involve parents in care and teach them how to support the child at home

Conclusion Love, security, acceptance, praise, independence and play are basic psychological needs of children; a nurse who meets them reduces the fear of hospitalisation and supports healthy development.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the factors affecting human development.
answer_html:
Introduction Human development is the orderly, progressive change in physical, mental, emotional and social abilities from conception to death. It is the result of the interaction of heredity and environment. Many factors decide how well a person develops.

1. Heredity

  • Genes from both parents decide physical features, potential for height and intelligence, temperament and sex
  • Genetic and chromosomal disorders (Down syndrome, thalassaemia, phenylketonuria) affect development

2. Prenatal (intra-uterine) environment

  • Mother's nutrition, anaemia and iodine deficiency
  • Infections during pregnancy – rubella, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, syphilis, HIV
  • Drugs, alcohol and smoking (alcohol may cause fetal alcohol syndrome), radiation, maternal stress, very young or old maternal age

3. Nutrition after birth

  • Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months and adequate complementary feeding are essential
  • Protein-energy malnutrition leads to stunting and poor brain development; iodine deficiency can cause cretinism

4. Hormones (endocrine glands)

  • Growth hormone, thyroxine and sex hormones control growth and maturity
  • Hypothyroidism in infancy causes delayed growth and intellectual disability if untreated

5. Health and illness

  • Repeated infections, worm infestation, chronic diseases and disabilities slow development

6. Family environment

  • Love, care and stimulation by parents; parenting style; family size, birth order and sibling relationships
  • Broken families, neglect and abuse harm emotional development

7. Socio-economic status

  • Poverty brings poor nutrition, crowded housing, poor sanitation and fewer chances of education

8. Education and stimulation

  • Talking, playing and reading with the child, pre-school (anganwadi) and school education develop language and intelligence

9. Culture, religion and society

  • Beliefs, food practices, gender roles and child-rearing customs influence development

10. Sex

  • Girls usually reach puberty and maturity earlier than boys

11. Physical environment and life events

  • Pollution, climate, disasters, trauma and peer and media influences

12. Emotional climate, exercise and rest

  • A child who feels loved and secure develops better than one living with fear, quarrels or abuse
  • Adequate play, physical activity and sleep are necessary for normal growth; growth hormone is secreted mainly during deep sleep

Nursing importance

  • Antenatal care, immunisation, growth monitoring, nutrition education, early stimulation and timely referral of children with delayed milestones

Conclusion Development depends on heredity and on many environmental factors – nutrition, health, family, education and socio-economic status; nurses can improve many of these through health care and education.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Describe the psychological needs of the elderly and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction In India, a person aged 60 years and above is called a senior citizen. Old age brings physical decline, retirement, loss of spouse and friends, reduced income and dependence on others. These changes create special psychological needs.

Psychological needs of the elderly

1. Security

  • Financial security, a safe place to live and assurance of care when ill
  • Fear of becoming a burden on children is common

2. Love, companionship and belonging

  • Loneliness is common after the death of a spouse or when children move to cities or abroad
  • They need family contact, friends and social groups

3. Respect and self-esteem

  • They want to be treated with dignity, consulted in family matters and valued for their experience

4. Independence

  • They wish to manage their own daily activities and decisions as long as possible

5. Meaningful activity

  • Hobbies, light work, grandparenting, religious and social activities give a sense of purpose

6. Communication

  • They need someone to listen to them and their memories (reminiscence)

7. Spiritual needs

  • Prayer, religious practices and preparing peacefully for death

Common psychological problems: loneliness, depression, anxiety, insomnia, dementia, fear of death and elder abuse or neglect. Depression in the elderly is often missed because it shows as body aches, poor appetite and poor sleep rather than sadness.

Role of the nurse

  • Address them respectfully (by name, "Aaji", "Uncle"), never in a childish way; be patient and give extra time
  • Speak slowly and clearly, face the person, and make sure spectacles and hearing aids are in use
  • Encourage self-care and allow them to make decisions about their own care
  • Encourage family visits, social contact, hobbies and senior citizens' groups and day-care centres
  • Use reminiscence – let them talk about their life and achievements
  • Screen for depression, memory loss and signs of abuse; refer when needed
  • Ensure safety – good lighting, non-slip floors, support rails – to prevent falls
  • Respect religious and spiritual practices
  • Inform them about services such as the National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly and pension schemes
  • Counsel the family about the needs and normal changes of ageing

Conclusion The elderly need security, companionship, respect, independence and purpose; a patient, respectful nurse can meet these needs and help them age with dignity.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define development. Explain Erikson's stages of psychosocial development and the role of the nurse in supporting normal development across the life span. (2 + 6 + 2)

diagram.caption: Erikson's eight psychosocial stages across the life span

answer_html:
(a) Definition of development (2 marks)

  • Development is the orderly, progressive series of changes in function, skill and behaviour that leads to maturity
  • It includes physical, cognitive (mental), emotional, social and moral development
  • It continues from conception to death – this is called life-span development
  • Principles: it is continuous; follows an orderly sequence; proceeds from head to foot (cephalocaudal) and from centre to periphery (proximodistal); moves from general to specific; has critical periods; and every individual develops at his own rate

(b) Erikson's stages of psychosocial development (6 marks) Erik Erikson, a German-American psychoanalyst, described eight stages from birth to old age. At each stage the person faces a psychosocial crisis (a conflict between two tendencies). When the crisis is resolved well, the person gains a strength (virtue); when it is not, problems carry over into later life.

1. Trust vs mistrust (birth – 1½ years)

  • The infant depends fully on the caregiver
  • Prompt, loving and consistent care (feeding, warmth, cuddling) → trust in the world → virtue: hope
  • Neglect or inconsistent care → mistrust, fear and suspicion

2. Autonomy vs shame and doubt (1½ – 3 years)

  • The toddler learns to walk, feed himself and use the toilet
  • Encouragement to do things for himself → autonomy → virtue: will
  • Over-protection, harsh toilet training or ridicule → shame and self-doubt

3. Initiative vs guilt (3 – 6 years)

  • The pre-schooler plays, explores, plans activities and asks endless questions
  • Encouragement → initiative → virtue: purpose
  • Frequent scolding or punishment → guilt and fear of trying new things

4. Industry vs inferiority (6 – 12 years)

  • The school child learns skills, completes tasks and compares himself with classmates
  • Success and praise → industry (competence) → virtue: competence
  • Repeated failure or criticism → inferiority

5. Identity vs role confusion (12 – 18 years)

  • The adolescent asks "Who am I?" – about career, values, beliefs and sexuality
  • A clear sense of self → identity → virtue: fidelity
  • Failure → role confusion, uncertainty and risk behaviour

6. Intimacy vs isolation (young adulthood, 18 – 40 years)

  • Forming close relationships, friendship, marriage
  • Success → intimacy → virtue: love
  • Failure → isolation and loneliness

7. Generativity vs stagnation (middle adulthood, 40 – 65 years)

  • Caring for children and the next generation, productive work, contributing to society
  • Success → generativity → virtue: care
  • Failure → stagnation, self-centredness

8. Ego integrity vs despair (late adulthood, 65 years onwards)

  • Looking back on life
  • Satisfaction with life → integrity → virtue: wisdom; accepts death calmly
  • Regret and bitterness → despair and fear of death

Summary table

Stage Age Crisis Virtue
Infancy 0 – 1½ yr trust vs mistrust hope
Toddler 1½ – 3 yr autonomy vs shame, doubt will
Pre-school 3 – 6 yr initiative vs guilt purpose
School age 6 – 12 yr industry vs inferiority competence
Adolescence 12 – 18 yr identity vs role confusion fidelity
Young adult 18 – 40 yr intimacy vs isolation love
Middle adult 40 – 65 yr generativity vs stagnation care
Old age 65+ yr integrity vs despair wisdom

Erikson compared with Freud's psychosexual stages

Age Freud (psychosexual) Erikson (psychosocial)
0 – 1½ yr oral – pleasure from sucking, feeding trust vs mistrust
1½ – 3 yr anal – toilet training autonomy vs shame and doubt
3 – 6 yr phallic – Oedipus / Electra complex initiative vs guilt
6 – 12 yr latency – sexual interest quiet industry vs inferiority
12 yr + genital – mature sexuality identity vs role confusion, and three adult stages
  • Freud stopped at adolescence and stressed sexual drives; Erikson covered the whole life span and stressed social relationships

Importance of Erikson's theory in nursing

  • Helps the nurse assess whether a patient's behaviour suits his age
  • Explains why illness at a particular age causes particular worries – the adolescent worries about appearance and friends, the middle-aged adult about family and job, the elderly about dependence and death
  • Guides age-appropriate care plans and health education

(c) Role of the nurse in supporting normal development (2 marks)

  • Infant – consistent caregiver, rooming-in, prompt response to crying, breastfeeding, cuddling
  • Toddler – allow self-feeding and simple choices; be patient with toilet training; avoid shaming
  • Pre-school child – provide play, answer questions, explain procedures with dolls; never threaten
  • School-age child – continue schoolwork, give small tasks, praise achievements
  • Adolescent – respect privacy, give honest information, involve in decisions, confidential counselling on body changes, career and risk behaviour
  • Young and middle adults – involve spouse and family, respect work and parenting roles, counsel on stress and lifestyle
  • Elderly – respect, reminiscence, encourage independence, support peaceful acceptance of death
  • At every age: health education to parents, growth monitoring and early referral when development is delayed

Conclusion Development is a life-long process. Erikson's eight stages show that each age has its own crisis and strength; by meeting the needs of each stage, the nurse helps patients develop and cope in a healthy way.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: List the principles of growth and development.
answer_html:
Introduction Growth and development follow certain general principles:

  1. Continuous and orderly – from conception to death, in a definite sequence
  2. Cephalocaudal direction – from head to toe (head control comes before sitting and walking)
  3. Proximodistal direction – from the centre to the periphery (arm movements before finger skills)
  4. From general to specific – mass movements first, then specific skills
  5. Individual differences – each child develops at his own rate
  6. Different rates for different parts – the brain grows fastest in early childhood; the reproductive organs at puberty
  7. Predictable pattern
  8. Result of heredity (maturation) and environment (learning)
  9. Critical periods – times when a particular development occurs most easily
  10. All aspects are interrelated – physical, mental, emotional and social development affect one another

subject: Applied Psychology
question: What are developmental tasks?
answer_html:
Definition Developmental tasks (Robert Havighurst) are tasks that arise at a particular period of life; successful achievement leads to happiness and success with later tasks, while failure leads to unhappiness, disapproval by society and difficulty with later tasks.

Sources: physical maturation, expectations of society and the person's own values.

Examples

  • Infancy and early childhood – learning to walk, eat solid food, talk, control bladder and bowel
  • Middle childhood – reading and writing, skills for games, getting along with peers
  • Adolescence – accepting one's body, emotional independence from parents, preparing for a career and marriage
  • Early adulthood – choosing a partner, starting a family, starting an occupation
  • Middle age – civic responsibility, helping teenagers, caring for ageing parents
  • Old age – adjusting to retirement, declining health and death of a spouse

Nursing: assess whether age-appropriate tasks are achieved and guide families.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Differentiate between maturation and learning.
answer_html:
Introduction Both bring changes in behaviour, but in different ways.

Maturation Learning
natural unfolding of abilities due to growth of the body and nervous system relatively permanent change in behaviour due to practice and experience
depends on heredity depends on environment and training
occurs in the same sequence in all varies from person to person
cannot be hurried by training improved by motivation and practice
e.g. sitting, walking, puberty changes e.g. reading, cycling, nursing skills

Relationship: learning depends on maturation (readiness) – e.g. toilet training succeeds only when the child is mature enough (usually around 18–24 months); training given too early is wasted.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain Piaget's theory of cognitive development.
answer_html:
Introduction Jean Piaget, a Swiss psychologist, explained how children's thinking (cognition) develops. He held that children actively build knowledge by exploring their world and that thinking develops through four stages in a fixed order.

Key concepts

  • Schema – a mental pattern for understanding something
  • Assimilation – fitting a new experience into an existing schema
  • Accommodation – changing a schema to fit new information
  • Equilibration – balancing assimilation and accommodation, which moves the child to higher levels of thinking

Stages of cognitive development

1. Sensorimotor stage (birth – 2 years)

  • Learns through the senses and movements – sucking, grasping, looking, listening
  • Develops object permanence – understands that objects exist even when out of sight (usually towards the end of the first year)
  • Begins imitation and simple symbolic thought

2. Pre-operational stage (2 – 7 years)

  • Rapid growth of language and symbolic (pretend) play
  • Egocentrism – cannot see things from another's point of view
  • Animism – believes lifeless objects are alive
  • Centration and lack of conservation – thinks a tall, thin glass holds more water than a short, wide one
  • Magical thinking – may believe illness is a punishment

3. Concrete operational stage (7 – 11 years)

  • Logical thinking about concrete (real) objects
  • Understands conservation, reversibility, classification and serial ordering
  • Less egocentric; understands cause and effect

4. Formal operational stage (11 – 12 years onwards)

  • Abstract and hypothetical thinking; deductive reasoning
  • Thinks about the future, possibilities and moral issues; scientific problem-solving

Application in nursing

  • Infants – sensory stimulation; keep the mother nearby (separation distress)
  • Preschool children – simple words, dolls and play to explain procedures; reassure that illness is not a punishment; avoid frightening words such as "cut"
  • School-age children – explain with pictures and models; let them handle equipment; involve them in self-care
  • Adolescents – full explanations, involvement in decisions, respect for privacy

Criticism

  • May have underestimated children's abilities
  • Gave little weight to culture and social interaction (stressed by Vygotsky)

Piaget on moral development (in brief)

  • Heteronomous morality (up to about 10 years) – rules are fixed and made by adults; actions are judged by their consequences (breaking many cups by accident seems worse than breaking one on purpose)
  • Autonomous morality (later) – rules can be changed by agreement; the intention behind an action matters

Conclusion Piaget described four stages – sensorimotor, pre-operational, concrete operational and formal operational – through which children's thinking grows from sensory exploration to abstract reasoning; nurses use these stages to communicate with children at their level.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Describe the developmental characteristics and problems of adolescence, and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Adolescence (from the Latin "adolescere" – to grow up) is the period of transition from childhood to adulthood, between 10 and 19 years (WHO). Stanley Hall called it a period of "storm and stress". About one-fifth of India's population is adolescent.

A. Developmental characteristics

  1. Physical – growth spurt, puberty and secondary sexual characters
  2. Cognitive – abstract, idealistic thinking; questioning of rules; adolescent egocentrism – feeling that everyone is watching them ("imaginary audience") and that nothing bad can happen to them ("personal fable")
  3. Emotional – intense, changing emotions; mood swings; sensitivity to criticism; desire for independence
  4. Social – peer group becomes very important; interest in the opposite sex; hero worship; conflict with parents (generation gap)
  5. Identity formation – Erikson's stage of identity versus role confusion
  6. Moral – develops personal values

B. Problems of adolescence

  • Identity confusion, low self-esteem, worry about body image (acne, weight, height)
  • Academic stress, examination anxiety, confusion about career
  • Emotional problems – anxiety, depression
  • Substance use – tobacco, alcohol, drugs
  • Risky sexual behaviour – teenage pregnancy, sexually transmitted infections, early marriage
  • Nutritional problems – anaemia (especially girls), undernutrition, obesity, eating disorders
  • Accidents and violence (road traffic injuries)
  • Mobile and internet addiction, cyberbullying
  • Juvenile delinquency
  • Menstrual problems and lack of menstrual hygiene

C. Role of the nurse

  • Health education – nutrition, weekly iron–folic acid, menstrual hygiene, reproductive and sexual health, dangers of substances, road and internet safety
  • Counselling – private, confidential and non-judgemental; build trust; listen
  • Adolescent-friendly health clinics under the Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK); peer educators; school health and wellness programmes
  • Guide parents – understanding, open communication, avoiding excessive control
  • Early identification and referral of depression, substance use and abuse
  • Life-skills training – decision-making, assertiveness, coping with stress

D. Life skills recommended by WHO

  • Self-awareness and empathy
  • Critical thinking and creative thinking
  • Decision-making and problem-solving
  • Effective communication and interpersonal relationships
  • Coping with stress and coping with emotions
  • These ten skills help adolescents handle peer pressure, conflicts and risky situations

Conclusion Adolescence brings rapid physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes and many problems such as identity confusion, stress, substance use and risky behaviour; the nurse supports adolescents through education, counselling, adolescent-friendly services and work with parents.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the psychological needs of a patient in sickness and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Illness and hospitalisation affect not only the body but also the mind. The adult patient faces fear, pain, loss of control, dependency and separation from family. Meeting the patient's psychological needs speeds recovery and improves cooperation. Common reactions include anxiety, irritability, regression and depression.

Psychological needs and the nurse's role

1. Need for security and safety

  • Fear of the unknown, pain, procedures and death
  • Nurse: orient the patient to the ward, explain procedures beforehand, keep the call bell within reach, respond promptly, give consistent care

2. Need for information

  • About the illness, treatment, progress and cost
  • Nurse: give clear, honest, simple information; arrange discussion with the doctor; obtain informed consent

3. Need for love, belonging and family contact

  • Separation from family causes loneliness
  • Nurse: allow suitable visiting, involve the family in care, permit phone calls

4. Need for self-esteem, dignity and respect

  • Exposure during examination and dependence for toileting and bathing hurt self-respect
  • Nurse: ensure privacy (screens, covering), address the patient by name, never by bed number or disease; encourage self-care

5. Need for independence and control

  • Nurse: involve the patient in decisions; offer choices (timing of bath, food preferences); encourage self-care as condition allows

6. Need to communicate and express feelings

  • Nurse: listen actively with empathy; allow the patient to express fear, anger or sadness without judging

7. Need to be treated as an individual

  • Nurse: give individualised care; respect culture, religion and habits

8. Need for hope and reassurance

  • Nurse: give realistic reassurance; point out progress; encourage

9. Need for spiritual comfort

  • Nurse: allow prayer and religious practices; arrange a visit by a religious leader if desired

10. Need for diversion

  • In long stays – reading, music, television, light occupational activities

11. Financial and occupational worries

  • Nurse: refer to the medical social worker; inform about schemes such as Ayushman Bharat (PM-JAY) and the Mahatma Jyotiba Phule Jan Arogya Yojana in Maharashtra

Assessing psychological needs

  • Observe behaviour, sleep, appetite and interaction with others
  • Ask open questions ("How are you feeling about the operation?")
  • Talk with the family about the patient's usual personality and worries
  • Use Maslow's hierarchy to set priorities – physical safety first, then emotional needs

Conclusion A sick adult needs security, information, love and family contact, dignity, independence, communication, hope and spiritual comfort; the nurse who meets these needs gives truly holistic care.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain Freud's psychosexual theory of personality development and its implications for nursing. (2 + 6 + 2)
answer_html:
(a) Introduction (2 marks)

  • Sigmund Freud (1856–1939), an Austrian neurologist, was the founder of psychoanalysis
  • He believed that personality is largely formed in the first five or six years of life
  • Development passes through five stages; in each, the libido (pleasure-seeking life energy) is centred on a different erogenous zone of the body
  • At each stage the child faces a conflict between its pleasure-seeking urges (the id) and the demands of parents and society
  • Fixation – if the needs of a stage are frustrated or over-indulged, the person may remain partly "stuck" there and show traits of that stage in adult life
  • Regression – under stress, a person may return to the behaviour of an earlier stage (e.g. a sick child wetting the bed again)
