Background concepts of Freud's theory (in brief)

  • Levels of the mind – like an iceberg:
    • conscious – what we are aware of now (the tip of the iceberg)
    • preconscious – memories that can be recalled easily
    • unconscious – the largest part; hidden wishes, fears and memories that still influence behaviour
  • Structure of personality:
    • id – present at birth; seeks immediate pleasure (pleasure principle)
    • ego – develops in the first years; deals with reality (reality principle)
    • superego – develops in the phallic stage; the conscience (morality principle)
  • The ego uses defence mechanisms to reduce the anxiety caused by conflicts between the id and the superego

(b) The psychosexual stages (6 marks)

1. Oral stage (birth – 1 year)

  • Zone: mouth – pleasure from sucking, feeding and biting
  • Key task: weaning; the infant depends completely on the mother and learns trust
  • Fixation: over-dependence, overeating, smoking, nail-biting, alcohol use, sarcasm

2. Anal stage (1 – 3 years)

  • Zone: anus – pleasure from holding and passing stools
  • Key task: toilet training – the first conflict with parental demands; the child learns self-control
  • Fixation:
    • anal-retentive (harsh training) – excessive orderliness, stubbornness, stinginess, perfectionism
    • anal-expulsive (lax training) – messiness, carelessness, disorganisation

3. Phallic stage (3 – 6 years)

  • Zone: genitals – the child becomes aware of sex differences
  • Oedipus complex (boys) – attachment to the mother and rivalry with the father; Electra complex (girls, term by Jung) – attachment to the father
  • Resolution: the child identifies with the parent of the same sex – this forms the superego (conscience) and gender role
  • Fixation: vanity, problems with authority, difficulties in relationships

4. Latency stage (6 years – puberty)

  • Sexual urges are dormant (repressed)
  • Energy goes into school, skills, hobbies, games and same-sex friendships
  • Development of social and intellectual skills

5. Genital stage (puberty onwards)

  • Sexual interest re-awakens and is directed towards partners outside the family
  • Mature adult – capable of love and productive work, balancing pleasure with responsibility

Summary table

Stage Age Focus Main task
Oral 0–1 year mouth feeding, weaning, trust
Anal 1–3 years anus toilet training, self-control
Phallic 3–6 years genitals identification with same-sex parent
Latency 6–12 years dormant school, skills, friendships
Genital puberty onwards mature sexuality love and work

Criticism

  • Over-emphasis on sex; ignores social and cultural influences
  • Based on memories of adult patients, not observation of children
  • Difficult to test scientifically; male-centred
  • Erikson later extended development across the whole life span, stressing social relationships

(c) Implications for nursing (2 marks)

  • Infants – meet oral needs: breastfeeding on demand, comforting by sucking during painful procedures, gentle weaning
  • Toddlers – patient, positive toilet training (never punish); accept regression (bed-wetting, thumb-sucking) during illness
  • Preschool children – answer questions about the body honestly; respect modesty; explain procedures on the genital area (e.g. catheterisation) carefully, as children of this age fear injury to the body
  • School-age children – provide schoolwork, games and peer contact in hospital
  • Adolescents – privacy, sex education and counselling
  • Adults – recognise defence mechanisms and regression during illness; understand that some behaviour has unconscious causes; build a therapeutic relationship
  • Elderly and chronically ill patients – may become dependent and demanding; accept this calmly and encourage independence step by step
  • Parents – counsel them on feeding, weaning, toilet training and answering children's questions about the body in a calm, matter-of-fact way

Conclusion Freud described five psychosexual stages – oral, anal, phallic, latency and genital – in which conflicts over bodily pleasures shape adult personality, with fixation leading to particular traits; though criticised, the theory helps nurses understand children's needs and patients' reactions to illness.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define personality.
answer_html:
Definition

  • The word comes from the Latin "persona" – the mask worn by actors in ancient theatre
  • Gordon Allport: "Personality is the dynamic organisation within the individual of those psychophysical systems that determine his unique adjustments to his environment."
  • In simple words, personality is the sum total of a person's physical, mental, emotional and social traits that make him unique

Features

  1. Unique – no two people are alike
  2. Consistent – fairly stable over time
  3. Dynamic – keeps developing
  4. Shaped by heredity and environment

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain id, ego and superego.
answer_html:
Introduction Sigmund Freud said personality has three parts that work together.

  1. Id – the primitive, unconscious part present from birth; contains instincts (hunger, sex, aggression); works on the pleasure principle – wants immediate satisfaction
  2. Ego – the rational, decision-making part; works on the reality principle; balances the demands of the id, the superego and the real world; uses defence mechanisms
  3. Superego – the moral part (conscience); develops from the values of parents and society; produces guilt when we do wrong

Healthy personality: a strong ego keeps the id and superego in balance.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Name the projective tests of personality.
answer_html:
Introduction Projective tests present an unclear (ambiguous) stimulus; the person "projects" his hidden feelings, needs and conflicts into the response.

Projective tests

  1. Rorschach inkblot test – 10 inkblot cards (Hermann Rorschach)
  2. Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) – the person makes up stories about pictures (Murray and Morgan)
  3. Children's Apperception Test (CAT) – pictures of animals for children
  4. Sentence completion test – "I feel happy when…"
  5. Word association test – first word that comes to mind
  6. Draw-a-person test

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Classify personality.
answer_html:
Introduction Psychologists have tried to group people into types that share common characteristics. These type theories are easy to understand, though in reality most people show a mixture of types.

1. Hippocrates – four temperaments (based on body fluids or "humours")

  • Sanguine (blood) – cheerful, hopeful, sociable, active
  • Choleric (yellow bile) – quick-tempered, irritable, ambitious
  • Melancholic (black bile) – sad, pessimistic, thoughtful
  • Phlegmatic (phlegm) – calm, slow, unemotional

2. Kretschmer – based on body build

  • Pyknic – short, stout; jolly, sociable, with mood swings
  • Asthenic (leptosomic) – tall, thin; shy, reserved, unsociable
  • Athletic – muscular, strong; energetic, active
  • Dysplastic – mixed, disproportionate build

3. Sheldon – body type (somatotype) and temperament

  • Endomorph – soft, round body; relaxed, loves food and comfort, sociable (viscerotonia)
  • Mesomorph – muscular body; energetic, bold, adventurous (somatotonia)
  • Ectomorph – thin, fragile body; sensitive, private, intellectual (cerebrotonia)

4. Carl Jung – psychological types

  • Introvert – reserved, prefers solitude, thinks before acting, sensitive
  • Extrovert – outgoing, talkative, sociable, action-oriented
  • Ambivert – shows both tendencies; most people belong here

5. Friedman and Rosenman – Type A and Type B

  • Type A – competitive, impatient, always in a hurry, easily angered; higher risk of coronary heart disease
  • Type B – relaxed, patient, easy-going

6. Trait approach

  • Describes personality by traits rather than fixed types
  • Allport – cardinal, central and secondary traits
  • Cattell – 16 personality factors (16 PF)
  • Big Five (OCEAN) – Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism

Summary table

Classification Basis Types
Hippocrates body fluids sanguine, choleric, melancholic, phlegmatic
Kretschmer body build pyknic, asthenic, athletic, dysplastic
Sheldon somatotype endomorph, mesomorph, ectomorph
Jung direction of interest introvert, extrovert, ambivert
Friedman & Rosenman behaviour pattern Type A, Type B
Trait theorists measurable traits 16 PF, Big Five

Limitations of type theories: people do not fit neatly into one type; they oversimplify personality and ignore the effect of environment and learning.

Nursing importance

  • An introverted patient may not express pain or worries, so the nurse must ask gently
  • Type A patients with heart disease need counselling on stress and anger control
  • Knowing types helps the nurse adjust communication and teaching

Conclusion Personality has been classified by temperament, body build, psychological type and traits; these classifications help nurses understand and respond to patients' individual differences.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the factors affecting personality development.
answer_html:
Introduction Personality is not inborn and fixed; it develops gradually from birth through the interaction of biological, psychological and social factors.

A. Biological factors

1. Heredity

  • Temperament, intelligence, physique and certain abilities are partly inherited
  • Twin studies show that identical twins are similar in many traits even when reared apart

2. Physique and appearance

  • Height, complexion, beauty or physical defects affect body image and self-confidence
  • A child teased for a defect may become shy and withdrawn

3. Endocrine glands

  • Thyroid – hyperthyroidism causes restlessness and irritability; hypothyroidism causes dullness and slowness
  • Adrenal – emotional reactions; pituitary – growth; gonads – sexual maturity and adolescent behaviour

4. Nervous system and health

  • Brain damage, chronic illness and disability can change personality

B. Psychological factors

  • Intelligence – helps in adjustment and problem-solving
  • Emotional maturity and control
  • Self-concept – how the person sees himself
  • Experiences of success and failure, motivation and interests

C. Environmental and social factors

1. Family – the most important influence

  • Parent–child relationship: love and acceptance build security; rejection or over-protection cause insecurity or dependence
  • Parenting style: authoritative (warm with limits) produces confident children; authoritarian (strict) may produce fearful or rebellious children; permissive may produce poor self-control
  • Birth order, sibling relationships, broken homes, family conflict

2. School and teachers

  • Discipline, encouragement, success in studies and sports, teacher as role model

3. Peer group

  • Especially in adolescence – dress, speech, habits, values

4. Culture and religion

  • Values, customs, gender roles, moral standards

5. Socio-economic status

  • Opportunities, nutrition, education and exposure

6. Mass media and social media

  • Role models, attitudes and lifestyle

7. Life experiences

  • Trauma, abuse, loss, migration or achievements can change personality

8. Adult roles

  • Occupation, marriage, parenthood and responsibilities continue to shape personality in adult life

9. Illness and hospitalisation

  • Long illness can make a person dependent, irritable or withdrawn; recovery and support restore confidence

Nursing importance

  • Educate parents about loving, consistent parenting; identify children with behaviour problems early; build patients' self-esteem

Conclusion Personality develops from the interaction of heredity, body, mind and environment, with the family playing the main role; a positive, supportive environment produces a well-adjusted personality.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define personality. Describe the methods of assessment of personality and the role of the nurse in identification and improvement of altered personality. (2 + 5 + 3)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Personality comes from the Latin word "persona", meaning mask
  • Allport (1937): "Personality is the dynamic organisation within the individual of those psychophysical systems that determine his unique adjustments to his environment"
  • It is the total pattern of a person's characteristic ways of thinking, feeling and behaving that makes him unique
  • It is unique, consistent, dynamic, and shaped by heredity and environment

(b) Methods of assessment of personality (5 marks) Personality assessment means measuring and evaluating the traits of a person. It is used in diagnosis, counselling, selection and research.

1. Observation

  • Watching the person's behaviour in natural or planned situations – how he talks, works, reacts to stress and relates to others
  • Merit: real-life behaviour; limitation: observer bias, time-consuming

2. Interview

  • Structured (fixed questions) or unstructured (free conversation)
  • Gives information about history, attitudes and feelings, along with non-verbal cues
  • Limitation: depends on the skill of the interviewer

3. Case history (biographical method)

  • Detailed life history from birth – family, school, work, illness, relationships – collected from the person, relatives and records

4. Self-report inventories (questionnaires)

  • The person answers a set of written questions about himself
  • Examples: MMPI (Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory), Cattell's 16 PF, Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ), Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI)
  • Merit: objective scoring, quick, can be used in groups
  • Limitation: person may fake answers to look good

5. Rating scales

  • Teachers, supervisors or family members rate the person on traits such as honesty, cooperation and leadership (e.g. a 5-point scale)
  • Limitation: halo effect – one good or bad trait influences the rating of all others

6. Projective techniques

  • An ambiguous stimulus is given, and the person projects his inner feelings:
    • Rorschach inkblot test – 10 cards; the person says what he sees
    • Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) – he makes up stories about pictures
    • Children's Apperception Test (CAT), sentence completion, word association, draw-a-person
  • Merit: reveals unconscious conflicts; difficult to fake
  • Limitation: interpretation is subjective and needs trained psychologists

7. Situational (behavioural) tests

  • The person is placed in a real-life-like situation – e.g. a leaderless group discussion or a stress task – and his behaviour is observed

Comparison

Method Main strength Main weakness
Observation natural behaviour observer bias
Inventory objective, quick faking
Rating scale uses people who know him halo effect
Projective test reveals unconscious subjective scoring

Characteristics of a good personality test

  • Reliable – consistent results on repetition
  • Valid – measures the traits it claims to measure
  • Standardised – same instructions, scoring and norms for all
  • Objective – scoring does not depend on the examiner's opinion
  • Practical – simple, economical and not too time-consuming

Uses of personality assessment

  • Clinical diagnosis of personality disorders and mental illness
  • Counselling and guidance of students and patients
  • Selection for jobs and training courses
  • Planning individualised care and therapy
  • Research on personality and behaviour

Alteration in personality

  • Personality disorders – long-standing rigid patterns such as paranoid, schizoid, antisocial, borderline, histrionic, dependent and obsessive-compulsive personality
  • Personality change due to head injury, dementia, brain tumour, epilepsy, alcohol and drug abuse, chronic illness or long hospitalisation (dependence, regression, irritability)

(c) Role of the nurse (3 marks)

Identification of personality and its alterations

  • Observe behaviour, communication, mood, relationships and reaction to illness
  • Take a history from the family – "Has his behaviour changed recently?"
  • Note sudden changes such as aggression, withdrawal or suspiciousness after illness, injury or drugs
  • Use simple rating scales and checklists; record observations objectively
  • Refer to the psychiatrist or psychologist for detailed assessment

Improvement of altered personality

  • Build a therapeutic relationship based on trust, acceptance and a non-judgemental attitude
  • Set consistent limits for manipulative or aggressive behaviour, with the whole team following the same rules
  • Use positive reinforcement – praise desirable behaviour
  • Encourage self-care, independence and decision-making to reduce dependence
  • Provide social skills training, group and recreational activities
  • Teach coping skills – relaxation, problem-solving, anger management
  • Counsel and involve the family; educate about avoiding alcohol and drugs
  • Act as a role model and maintain self-awareness of one's own reactions

Conclusion Personality is the unique, dynamic organisation of a person's traits. It is assessed by observation, interviews, inventories, rating scales, projective and situational tests. By identifying alterations early and using a supportive, consistent approach, the nurse helps patients develop a healthier personality.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Differentiate between character and temperament.
answer_html:
Introduction Both are parts of personality, but they differ.

Temperament Character
the emotional nature – a person's typical way of reacting emotionally (mood, activity, sensitivity) the moral and ethical side – values, honesty, integrity, habits of conduct
largely inborn (hereditary) acquired through upbringing, education and socialisation
seen early in infancy develops with age and experience
not judged good or bad judged good or bad
e.g. calm, irritable, cheerful, shy e.g. honest, disciplined, responsible, dishonest

Note: Thomas and Chess described easy, difficult and slow-to-warm-up temperaments in children.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define self-concept. Name its components.
answer_html:
Definition Self-concept is the total picture a person has of himself – his beliefs, ideas and feelings about who he is (Carl Rogers).

Components

  1. Body image – how one perceives one's own body and appearance
  2. Self-esteem – the value or worth one places on oneself
  3. Role performance – how well one fulfils expected roles (parent, worker, student)
  4. Personal identity – sense of being a unique, separate individual
  5. Ideal self – what one would like to be

Development: shaped by feedback from parents, teachers and peers, and by successes and failures.

Applied: illness and surgery – mastectomy, amputation, colostomy, burns – threaten body image and self-esteem; the nurse gives acceptance, support and rehabilitation.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain Carl Rogers' self theory of personality.
answer_html:
Introduction Carl Rogers (1902–1987), an American humanistic psychologist, developed person-centred (client-centred) therapy. His theory places the self at the centre of personality and holds that people are basically good and have an inborn tendency to grow.

Key concepts

1. Actualising tendency

  • An inborn drive in every person to grow, develop and fulfil his potential – leading towards self-actualisation

2. Self-concept

  • The organised set of perceptions and beliefs a person has about himself
  • Real self – what one actually is; ideal self – what one would like to be

3. Congruence and incongruence

  • Congruence – when the self-concept matches the person's actual experiences (and the real and ideal selves are close) → mental health
  • Incongruence – a mismatch → anxiety, defensiveness and maladjustment

4. Need for positive regard

  • Everyone needs love, acceptance and approval from others
  • Unconditional positive regard – being accepted and valued without conditions → healthy self-concept
  • Conditional positive regard ("conditions of worth") – being loved only when behaving as others wish → the person denies his true feelings → incongruence

5. Phenomenal field

  • Each person's own subjective world of experience; behaviour depends on how the person perceives reality, not on reality itself

6. Fully functioning person

  • The ideal of psychological health – open to experience, lives fully in the present, trusts his own feelings, feels free and is creative

Application in nursing

  • Client-centred approach – respect and unconditional acceptance of every patient, including those with HIV, addiction or a history of self-harm
  • Rogers' three core conditions of a helping relationship:
    • Empathy – understanding the patient's feelings from his point of view
    • Genuineness (congruence) – being honest and real
    • Unconditional positive regard – non-judgemental acceptance
  • Active listening and reflecting feelings in therapeutic communication
  • Promoting self-esteem and self-care; involving patients in decisions

Criticism

  • Too optimistic about human nature
  • Concepts are difficult to measure; neglects the unconscious and biological factors

Freud and Rogers compared

Freud Rogers
pessimistic view of human nature optimistic – people are basically good
behaviour driven by the unconscious behaviour guided by the conscious self
focus on the past (childhood) focus on the present and growth
therapist interprets therapist listens; the client leads

Conclusion Rogers' self theory explains personality through the self-concept, the actualising tendency, congruence and the need for positive regard; his core conditions of empathy, genuineness and unconditional positive regard are the basis of therapeutic nursing relationships.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the alterations of personality and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Alteration in personality means either a lasting change from a person's usual way of thinking, feeling and behaving, or a long-standing maladaptive pattern (personality disorder) that causes distress and problems in relationships and work.

A. Causes of personality change

  • Brain injury, especially of the frontal lobe – disinhibition, impulsiveness, apathy
  • Neurological diseases – dementia, brain tumours, stroke, epilepsy
  • Mental illness – schizophrenia, depression, mania
  • Substance abuse – alcohol and drugs
  • Endocrine disorders – hypothyroidism (slowness, apathy), hyperthyroidism (irritability)
  • Drugs – steroids
  • Severe stress and trauma, chronic illness, old age

B. Personality disorders Deeply ingrained, inflexible patterns that usually begin in adolescence or early adulthood. They are commonly grouped into three clusters:

  • Cluster A – odd, eccentric:
    • paranoid – suspicious, distrustful
    • schizoid – detached, cold, prefers to be alone
    • schizotypal – odd beliefs and behaviour
  • Cluster B – dramatic, emotional, erratic:
    • antisocial – disregards rules and others' rights, no guilt
    • borderline – unstable mood, relationships and self-image, impulsive, self-harm
    • histrionic – attention-seeking, dramatic
    • narcissistic – feels superior, needs admiration, lacks empathy
  • Cluster C – anxious, fearful:
    • avoidant – shy, fears rejection
    • dependent – excessive need to be cared for
    • obsessive-compulsive – perfectionist, rigid, over-controlled
  • (The newer ICD-11 describes personality disorder mainly by its severity – mild, moderate or severe.)

C. Common features

  • Rigid, inflexible behaviour; poor insight; repeated problems in relationships and work

D. Role of the nurse

  • Observe and assess behaviour; report sudden personality change, which may indicate brain disease or delirium
  • Build a therapeutic relationship – consistent, firm, fair limits; clear rules; avoid being manipulated; stay non-judgemental
  • Safety – watch for risk of self-harm or aggression
  • Help develop social skills, coping skills and self-esteem; reinforce positive behaviour
  • Educate and support the family
  • Refer for psychiatric care and psychotherapy; ensure medication compliance where prescribed
  • Self-awareness – do not take difficult behaviour personally; use a team approach

E. When a personality change needs urgent attention

  • Sudden change over hours or days, especially with confusion, fever, headache, a recent head injury or a new medicine – it may indicate delirium, infection, a bleed or a tumour and must be reported at once

Conclusion Personality may be altered by brain disease, mental illness, substances, hormones and stress, or may be disordered in a lasting way; the nurse observes changes, sets consistent limits, ensures safety, supports the family and refers for treatment.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Enumerate the determinants of attention.
answer_html:
Definition Attention is the process of focusing consciousness on one particular stimulus while ignoring others.

A. Objective (external) determinants – qualities of the stimulus

  1. Intensity and size – a loud alarm or a big poster
  2. Novelty – something new or unusual
  3. Change and movement – a flickering light, a moving object
  4. Contrast – a red word on a white page
  5. Repetition – an advertisement repeated often
  6. Colour and position – bright colours; items at the top or centre

B. Subjective (internal) determinants – conditions of the person

  1. Interest and needs (a hungry person notices food stalls)
  2. Mental set and expectations
  3. Emotions, habits and past experience
  4. Health and fatigue – a tired person cannot concentrate

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define learning.
answer_html:
Definition Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour that results from practice or experience.

Explanation

  • Changes due to maturation, fatigue, illness or drugs are not learning
  • Learning may be good or bad – a skill or a bad habit

Characteristics

  1. A continuous, life-long process
  2. Universal – everyone learns
  3. Goal-directed and purposeful
  4. Results from practice and experience
  5. Can be transferred to new situations

Types: motor learning (giving an injection), verbal learning (medical terms), concept learning, problem-solving and attitude learning.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define perception. List the Gestalt principles of perception.
answer_html:
Definition Perception is the process of selecting, organising and interpreting sensations to give them meaning. Sensation is receiving a stimulus; perception is understanding it.

Gestalt principles of perceptual organisation

  1. Figure–ground – we see an object (figure) standing out from its background
  2. Proximity – things close together are seen as a group
  3. Similarity – similar things (shape, colour) are grouped together
  4. Closure – we fill gaps to see a complete figure
  5. Continuity – we see smooth, continuous lines rather than broken ones
  6. Simplicity (Prägnanz) – we see the simplest possible form

Gestalt is a German word meaning "whole form" – the whole is more than the sum of its parts.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: State the causes of forgetting.
answer_html:
Definition Forgetting is the inability to recall or recognise something that was learnt earlier.

Causes

  1. Decay (disuse) – memory fades when not used; Ebbinghaus showed most forgetting happens soon after learning
  2. Interference – proactive (old learning blocks new) and retroactive (new learning blocks old)
  3. Repression (motivated forgetting) – painful memories pushed out of awareness
  4. Lack of retrieval cues – the memory is stored but cannot be reached
  5. Poor learning – inattention, cramming, no understanding
  6. Physical causes – head injury, ageing, dementia, alcohol, lack of sleep and stress

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the types of memory.

diagram.caption: Atkinson–Shiffrin model of memory (sensory → short-term → long-term)

answer_html:
Introduction Memory is the mental ability to receive (encode), store (retain) and recall (retrieve) information and past experiences. According to the Atkinson–Shiffrin model, information passes through three stores – sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory.

1. Sensory memory

  • Holds information from the senses for a very short time – less than one second for visual images and about 2–4 seconds for sounds
  • Iconic memory – visual (the image of a lightning flash)
  • Echoic memory – auditory (you can "replay" the last few words someone said)
  • Large capacity, but whatever is not attended to is lost

2. Short-term memory (working memory)

  • Holds information we are actively using, for about 15–30 seconds without rehearsal
  • Limited capacity – about 7 ± 2 items (George Miller)
  • Chunking increases capacity – a mobile number 98220 45116 is remembered as two chunks
  • Rehearsal (repeating) keeps it alive and helps transfer it to long-term memory
  • Example: remembering a patient's BP reading till you write it in the chart

3. Long-term memory

  • Stores information for long periods – even a lifetime; capacity is practically unlimited
  • (a) Explicit (declarative) memory – can be consciously recalled
    • Episodic memory – personal events with time and place ("my first day in the ward")
    • Semantic memory – facts and knowledge ("normal pulse is 60–100 per minute")
  • (b) Implicit (non-declarative) memory – used without conscious effort
    • Procedural memory – skills and habits (riding a bicycle, making a bed, typing)
    • Priming and conditioned responses

4. Other types of memory

  • Rote memory – learning by repetition without understanding; logical memory – learning with understanding, which lasts longer
  • Immediate, recent and remote memory – tested in mental status examination
  • Recall (reproducing without cues, as in an essay answer) and recognition (identifying from choices, as in MCQs)

Nursing importance

  • In dementia and head injury, recent memory is lost first while remote memory remains – patients need reminders, labels and routines
  • While teaching patients, give short chunks, repeat key points and provide written instructions
  • Nursing students learn better by understanding and practice than by rote

Conclusion Memory works in three stages – sensory, short-term and long-term – and long-term memory includes episodic, semantic and procedural memory. Understanding these helps nurses teach effectively and care for patients with memory problems.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Describe the factors influencing learning and the laws of learning.
answer_html:
Introduction Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour due to practice or experience. How well a person learns depends on the learner, the material, the method and the environment. E. L. Thorndike also gave laws that explain how learning takes place.

A. Factors influencing learning

1. Learner-related factors

  • Age and maturity – the learner must be physically and mentally ready
  • Intelligence – bright learners learn faster
  • Motivation and interest – the strongest factor; a motivated learner learns quickly
  • Physical health – illness, hunger, poor vision or hearing and fatigue reduce learning
  • Emotional state – anxiety, fear and depression block learning
  • Previous knowledge and experience – new learning builds on old

2. Material-related factors

  • Meaningful material is learnt faster than nonsense material
  • Length and difficulty – long, difficult content needs more time
  • Organisation – material arranged from simple to complex, known to unknown

3. Method-related factors

  • Spaced (distributed) practice is better than massed practice (cramming)
  • Whole vs part method – short, meaningful material by the whole method; long material in parts
  • Active participation – recitation, discussion, demonstration and return demonstration
  • Feedback and reinforcement – knowing results and receiving praise
  • Use of audio-visual aids

4. Environmental factors

  • Physical – good light, ventilation, quiet, comfortable seating
  • Social – teacher's attitude, classroom climate, peer group, family support

B. Thorndike's laws of learning

  1. Law of readiness – learning takes place best when the learner is ready (physically and mentally prepared); forcing an unready learner causes annoyance
  2. Law of exercise – practice strengthens learning (law of use); lack of practice weakens it (law of disuse)
  3. Law of effect – responses followed by satisfaction are strengthened; those followed by discomfort are weakened

Secondary laws: multiple response, mental set (attitude), analogy and associative shifting.

Nursing importance

  • Teach patients when they are ready – not when in severe pain or immediately after bad news
  • Give short sessions, demonstrate skills and ask for return demonstration (e.g. insulin injection)
  • Praise correct performance and repeat key points

Conclusion Learning depends on the learner, the material, the method and the environment; Thorndike's laws of readiness, exercise and effect guide effective teaching of students and patients.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the principles of perception and the factors affecting perception.
answer_html:
Introduction Perception is the process of selecting, organising and interpreting sensory information into meaningful experiences. Two persons may receive the same sensation but perceive it differently, because perception depends on the person as well as on the stimulus.

A. Principles of perception

1. Selectivity

  • Out of thousands of stimuli we perceive only a few – those we pay attention to

2. Perceptual organisation (Gestalt laws)

  • Figure–ground – an object stands out from its background
  • Proximity – nearby items are grouped
  • Similarity – similar items are grouped
  • Closure – incomplete figures are seen as complete
  • Continuity – smooth continuous patterns are preferred

3. Perceptual constancy

  • We see objects as stable even when the image on the retina changes
  • Size constancy (a person walking away does not "shrink"), shape constancy (a door seen at an angle still looks rectangular), colour and brightness constancy

4. Depth perception

  • Judging distance using binocular cues (two eyes – retinal disparity, convergence) and monocular cues (size, overlap, shadow, perspective)

B. Factors affecting perception

1. External (stimulus) factors

  • Intensity, size, contrast, movement, novelty and repetition of the stimulus

2. Internal (personal) factors

  • Needs and motives – a hungry person perceives food quickly
  • Past experience and learning – a nurse quickly perceives a change in a patient's breathing
  • Mental set and expectations – we perceive what we expect to see
  • Emotions – a frightened person may perceive a rope as a snake in the dark
  • Attitudes, values and culture
  • Physical state – fatigue, illness, drugs and alcohol distort perception

C. Errors of perception

  • Illusion – wrong perception of a real stimulus (Müller-Lyer lines of equal length appear unequal)
  • Hallucination – perception without any stimulus (hearing voices when no one is speaking), seen in psychosis and delirium

Nursing importance

  • Pain perception differs with culture, fear and past experience, so the nurse accepts the patient's report of pain
  • Reduce misperceptions in ICU and in the elderly with good lighting, orientation and explanation
  • Patients may perceive the nurse's tone and facial expression more than her words

Conclusion Perception is selective and organised by principles such as figure–ground, proximity and closure; it is influenced by stimulus factors and by the person's needs, experience, emotions and culture.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Describe the types of thinking and the steps in problem solving.
answer_html:
Introduction Thinking is a mental process of using ideas, images and symbols to understand, reason, solve problems and make decisions. It is the highest cognitive process and is closely linked with language, memory and intelligence.

A. Elements of thinking

  • Images (mental pictures), concepts (general ideas such as "fever"), symbols and language

B. Types of thinking

1. Perceptual (concrete) thinking

  • Thinking about objects that are present and can be seen or touched; common in children

2. Conceptual (abstract) thinking

  • Thinking with concepts and ideas that are not physically present, e.g. "justice", "health"

3. Reflective (logical) thinking

  • Careful, step-by-step reasoning to solve a problem

4. Creative thinking

  • Producing new and original ideas, e.g. designing a new low-cost splint

5. Critical thinking

  • Questioning, analysing and evaluating information before accepting it – essential in clinical decisions

6. Convergent and divergent thinking

  • Convergent – arriving at one correct answer (an MCQ); divergent – producing many possible answers (ways to prevent falls in a ward)

7. Associative (autistic) thinking

  • Free, uncontrolled flow of ideas as in day-dreaming

C. Reasoning

  • Inductive reasoning – from particular cases to a general rule
  • Deductive reasoning – from a general rule to a particular case

D. Steps in problem solving

  1. Identify and define the problem clearly
  2. Collect information about it
  3. Generate possible solutions (alternatives)
  4. Evaluate each solution – advantages, disadvantages and feasibility
  5. Choose the best solution
  6. Implement (carry it out)
  7. Evaluate the result; if the problem remains, start again

E. Barriers to problem solving

  • Mental set (sticking to old methods), functional fixedness (seeing an object only in its usual use), lack of information, emotional stress and fatigue

Nursing importance

  • The nursing process – assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation – is a form of problem solving
  • Critical thinking helps nurses make safe clinical judgements and recognise early changes in a patient's condition

Conclusion Thinking may be concrete, abstract, logical, creative or critical, and problem solving follows systematic steps; these skills form the basis of the nursing process and safe practice.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define intelligence. Explain the factors influencing intelligence and the measurement of intelligence (IQ). (2 + 4 + 4)

diagram.caption: Normal distribution of IQ scores in the population

answer_html:
(a) Definition of intelligence (2 marks)

  • David Wechsler: intelligence is "the aggregate or global capacity of the individual to act purposefully, to think rationally and to deal effectively with his environment"
  • Alfred Binet: the ability to judge well, understand well and reason well
  • Terman: the ability to carry on abstract thinking
  • In simple words, intelligence is the ability to learn, understand, reason, solve problems and adjust to new situations

Theories of intelligence (in brief)

  • Spearman's two-factor theory – a general factor (g) used in all tasks and specific factors (s) for particular tasks
  • Thurstone – seven primary mental abilities: verbal comprehension, word fluency, number, space, memory, perceptual speed and reasoning
  • Howard Gardner – multiple intelligences: linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal and naturalistic
  • Emotional intelligence (Daniel Goleman) – the ability to understand and manage one's own emotions and those of others; very important for nurses

(b) Factors influencing intelligence (4 marks) Intelligence is the result of the interaction of heredity and environment.

1. Heredity

  • Intelligence potential is partly inherited; identical twins have more similar IQs than fraternal twins, even when reared apart
  • Bright parents tend to have bright children, though there are many exceptions

2. Prenatal and birth factors

  • Maternal malnutrition, iodine deficiency, infections (rubella), alcohol and drugs in pregnancy
  • Birth asphyxia, prematurity and neonatal jaundice (kernicterus) can damage the brain

3. Nutrition

  • Protein-energy malnutrition, iron-deficiency anaemia and iodine deficiency in childhood lower intelligence

4. Home environment and stimulation

  • Talking, reading, playing and encouragement from parents improve intelligence
  • Neglected, unstimulated children score lower

5. Education and opportunities

  • Schooling, books, travel and exposure develop intellectual ability

6. Socio-economic status

  • Poverty brings poor nutrition, poor health and fewer learning opportunities

7. Health and disease

  • Hypothyroidism (cretinism), phenylketonuria, meningitis, epilepsy, head injury and lead poisoning reduce intelligence

8. Age

  • Intelligence grows rapidly in childhood and reaches its peak in late adolescence or early adulthood; some abilities (speed, memory) decline in old age while knowledge and judgement remain

9. Sex, race and culture

  • There is no overall difference in intelligence between the sexes or races; differences in test scores are mainly due to environment, education and culture-biased tests

10. Emotional and motivational factors

  • Anxiety, low motivation and poor attention lower test performance

(c) Measurement of intelligence (IQ) (4 marks)

1. Mental age (MA)

  • Alfred Binet (1905, with Simon) developed the first intelligence test and introduced the idea of mental age – the age level at which a person performs

2. Intelligence quotient (IQ)

  • The term was given by William Stern; it was popularised by Lewis Terman in the Stanford–Binet test (1916)
  • IQ = (Mental age ÷ Chronological age) × 100
  • Example: a child aged 8 years (CA) who performs like a 10-year-old (MA): IQ = 10 ÷ 8 × 100 = 125
  • For adults, the deviation IQ (Wechsler) is used – the average score is set at 100 with a standard deviation of 15

3. Classification of IQ

IQ Category
140 and above genius / very superior
120 – 139 superior
110 – 119 high average (bright)
90 – 109 average
80 – 89 low average (dull)
70 – 79 borderline
below 70 intellectual disability

Levels of intellectual disability: mild (50–69), moderate (35–49), severe (20–34) and profound (below 20).

4. Distribution of IQ

  • IQ scores follow a normal (bell-shaped) curve: about 68% of people score between 85 and 115 and about 95% between 70 and 130

5. Types of intelligence tests

  • Individual tests – one person at a time: Stanford–Binet; Wechsler scales (WAIS for adults, WISC for children); in India, Bhatia's Battery of Performance Tests and Malin's Intelligence Scale for Indian Children
  • Group tests – many persons at a time: Army Alpha (verbal) and Army Beta (non-verbal)
  • Verbal tests – need reading and language
  • Non-verbal (performance) tests – use pictures, blocks and puzzles; useful for illiterate persons and children: Raven's Progressive Matrices, Seguin Form Board, Draw-a-Man test (Goodenough)

Nursing importance

  • Adjust health teaching to the patient's level of understanding
  • Recognise delayed milestones and refer children for early assessment and stimulation
  • Promote prevention of intellectual disability through iodised salt, antenatal care, safe delivery and newborn screening for hypothyroidism
  • Care of persons with intellectual disability with patience, simple instructions and training in self-care

Conclusion Intelligence is the global ability to think, learn and adjust. It is shaped by heredity and environment, measured as IQ (MA/CA × 100) with standardised tests, and classified from intellectual disability to genius – knowledge that helps nurses in teaching, early detection and prevention.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define memory. Explain the types of memory and the factors influencing memory. (2 + 4 + 4)

diagram.caption: Ebbinghaus forgetting curve – retention falls rapidly at first, then slowly

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Memory is the mental capacity to encode, store, retain and later recall or recognise information and past experiences
  • Woodworth: memory is remembering what has been learnt
  • Without memory there would be no learning, no skills and no sense of personal identity

Stages (process) of memory

  1. Encoding (registration) – taking in and processing information through attention and learning
  2. Storage (retention) – keeping the information over time
  3. Retrieval – bringing it back when needed by recall (essay answers), recognition (MCQs) or relearning (re-learning is faster the second time – the "savings" method of Ebbinghaus)

(b) Types of memory (4 marks)

1. Sensory memory

  • Holds sensory impressions for less than a second (iconic, visual) to a few seconds (echoic, auditory)

2. Short-term (working) memory

  • Holds about 7 ± 2 items for 15–30 seconds; lost if not rehearsed
  • Example: remembering a drug dose while preparing it

3. Long-term memory

  • Practically unlimited and long-lasting
  • Explicit (declarative): episodic (personal events – the day of your capping ceremony) and semantic (facts – the normal haemoglobin value)
  • Implicit (non-declarative): procedural memory for skills and habits (making an occupied bed)

4. Other classifications

  • Rote vs logical memory – memorising without vs with understanding
  • Immediate, recent and remote memory – tested by asking the patient to repeat numbers, recall breakfast and recall childhood events
  • Active (deliberate) vs passive (spontaneous) memory

(c) Factors influencing memory (4 marks)

A. Factors related to the learner

  • Attention and interest – what is attended to is remembered
  • Motivation and the will to remember
  • Intelligence and previous knowledge
  • Age – memory is best in youth; recent memory declines in old age
  • Physical health, sleep and nutrition – sleep helps consolidate memories; fatigue and hunger impair them
  • Emotional state – mild arousal helps, but severe anxiety, stress or depression impairs memory
  • Drugs, alcohol, head injury and brain diseases (dementia, stroke) cause memory loss

B. Factors related to the material

  • Meaningful material is retained better than meaningless material
  • Amount and difficulty of material
  • Organisation – well-organised material is remembered better
  • Vividness – unusual, colourful or emotionally striking material is remembered
  • Serial position effect – items at the beginning (primacy) and end (recency) of a list are remembered better than those in the middle

C. Factors related to the method of learning

  • Spaced learning is better than cramming
  • Recitation (self-testing) is better than repeated reading
  • Overlearning – continuing practice after mastery improves retention
  • Understanding (logical learning) is better than rote learning
  • Association with what is already known

D. Environmental factors

  • Quiet, distraction-free surroundings during learning
  • Context – recall is better in the same setting in which learning occurred
  • Interference from similar material learnt before or after

Forgetting

  • Ebbinghaus found that forgetting is fastest in the first few hours after learning and then slows down (forgetting curve)
  • Causes: decay through disuse; interference – proactive (old learning disturbs new, e.g. an old phone number blocks the new one) and retroactive (new learning disturbs old); repression of painful memories; retrieval failure (tip-of-the-tongue); poor original learning; and organic causes
  • Amnesia (loss of memory due to brain causes):
    • Retrograde – loss of memory for events before an injury
    • Anterograde – inability to form new memories after the injury
  • Forgetting is not always harmful – forgetting unpleasant and useless details keeps the mind efficient

Methods to improve memory

  • Pay full attention; understand before memorising
  • Revise at intervals – after one day, one week and one month (to beat the forgetting curve)
  • Use mnemonics – e.g. "ABC" (airway, breathing, circulation); "DABDA" for stages of dying
  • Make diagrams, flow charts and mind maps
  • Use chunking and association
  • Recite aloud and teach others
  • Get adequate sleep, eat well, exercise and avoid alcohol
  • Avoid last-minute cramming

Nursing importance

  • For elderly and dementia patients: calendars, clocks, labelled doors, pill organisers, a fixed routine and familiar persons
  • While teaching patients: speak simply, give one point at a time, repeat, and provide written or pictorial instructions; involve the family
  • Nurses must not depend on memory for drug doses or readings – record immediately

Conclusion Memory is the ability to encode, store and retrieve information. It has sensory, short-term and long-term types, and is influenced by the learner, the material, the method and the environment. Good study habits improve memory, and nurses use this knowledge in teaching and in caring for patients with memory problems.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define learning. Explain the theories of learning and their application in nursing. (2 + 6 + 2)

diagram.caption: Pavlov's classical conditioning – before, during and after conditioning

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour resulting from practice or experience
  • Changes due to growth, maturation, fatigue, illness or drugs are not learning
  • Learning process: motivation → goal → obstacle → trial responses → success → reinforcement → repetition → habit
  • Types: motor, verbal, concept, problem-solving and attitude learning

(b) Theories of learning (6 marks)

1. Trial and error learning – E. L. Thorndike

  • Experiment: a hungry cat was placed in a puzzle box with fish outside; the cat made many random movements and accidentally pressed a lever that opened the door. In later trials, useless movements decreased and the time to escape became shorter
  • Principle: learning takes place by trying, making errors and fixing the successful response
  • Laws: readiness, exercise and effect
  • Example: a student nurse learning to insert an IV cannula improves with each attempt

2. Classical conditioning – Ivan Pavlov (Russian physiologist)

  • Experiment: food (unconditioned stimulus, UCS) naturally produced salivation (unconditioned response, UCR) in a dog. A bell (neutral stimulus) was rung just before giving food. After repeated pairing, the bell alone (conditioned stimulus, CS) produced salivation (conditioned response, CR)
  • Principle: learning by association of two stimuli
  • Related terms:
    • Extinction – the CR disappears when the bell is repeatedly given without food
    • Spontaneous recovery – the CR suddenly reappears after a rest period
    • Generalisation – responding to similar stimuli (a child afraid of a doctor's white coat fears every person in white)
    • Discrimination – responding only to the specific stimulus
  • J. B. Watson showed that fears can be learnt in this way (the "Little Albert" experiment)

3. Operant (instrumental) conditioning – B. F. Skinner

  • Experiment: a hungry rat in a Skinner box pressed a lever by chance and received food; it soon learnt to press the lever often
  • Principle: behaviour is controlled by its consequences
    • Positive reinforcement – adding something pleasant (praise, reward) increases the behaviour
    • Negative reinforcement – removing something unpleasant (pain relief after taking medicine) increases the behaviour
    • Punishment – an unpleasant consequence decreases the behaviour
    • Extinction – behaviour stops when reinforcement stops
  • Schedules of reinforcement – continuous, fixed ratio, variable ratio, fixed interval and variable interval
  • Shaping – rewarding small steps towards the desired behaviour

4. Insight learning – Wolfgang Köhler (Gestalt school)

  • Experiment: a chimpanzee named Sultan could not reach bananas kept outside his cage; after some time he suddenly joined two sticks to pull the bananas in
  • Principle: learning by sudden understanding of the relationship between the parts of a problem – the "aha" experience
  • Example: a nurse suddenly understands how all the signs of a patient fit together into a diagnosis

5. Observational (social) learning – Albert Bandura

  • Experiment: children who watched an adult hit a Bobo doll later imitated the same aggressive behaviour
  • Principle: learning by observing and imitating models
  • Four processes: attention → retention → reproduction → motivation
  • Example: student nurses learn attitudes and skills by watching senior nurses and teachers

Comparison

Theory Psychologist Learning by Experiment
Trial and error Thorndike repeated attempts cat in puzzle box
Classical conditioning Pavlov association of stimuli dog and bell
Operant conditioning Skinner consequences (reinforcement) rat in Skinner box
Insight Köhler sudden understanding chimpanzee and sticks
Social learning Bandura observation and imitation Bobo doll

Transfer of learning

  • Positive transfer – earlier learning helps new learning (knowledge of anatomy helps in learning physiology; riding a bicycle helps in learning to ride a scooter)
  • Negative transfer – earlier learning interferes with new learning (a nurse used to one type of infusion pump makes errors with a new model)
  • Zero transfer – no effect
  • Teachers improve positive transfer by linking new topics with known ones and by teaching principles rather than isolated facts

Learning curve

  • A graph of progress against practice; learning is usually fast at first, then slows, and may show a plateau (a flat stage of no visible progress) before improving again – learners should not lose heart at the plateau

Habit formation

  • A habit is a learnt behaviour that becomes automatic through repetition
  • Good habits (hand hygiene, regular exercise) are formed by repetition, reinforcement and a strong start; bad habits are broken by replacing them with a better response

(c) Application in nursing (2 marks)

  • Patient teaching – demonstrate, allow practice and return demonstration (trial and error); praise correct performance (reinforcement)
  • Paediatric care – avoid painful associations; praise and small rewards build cooperation
  • Behaviour modification in psychiatric wards – token economy, positive reinforcement of self-care and social behaviour
  • Systematic desensitisation for phobias and fear of procedures (based on classical conditioning)
  • Role modelling – nurses are models for students and patients (social learning)
  • Health habits – forming habits such as hand washing, regular medication and exercise
  • Problem-solving and critical thinking in clinical situations (insight)

Conclusion Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour due to experience. Thorndike, Pavlov, Skinner, Köhler and Bandura explained learning through trial and error, association, reinforcement, insight and observation; nurses apply these theories daily in teaching, behaviour change and role modelling.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain attention – its types, characteristics and importance in nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Attention is the process of selecting and focusing the mind on one stimulus or task out of the many present, while ignoring others. It is the first step of perception, learning and memory – we cannot learn or remember what we do not attend to. It is influenced by external factors (intensity, novelty, movement of the stimulus) and internal factors (interest, needs, mood).

A. Types of attention

1. According to effort

  • Voluntary (active) attention – given deliberately, with effort, guided by goals – e.g. studying for an examination, checking a drug dose
  • Involuntary (passive) attention – drawn without effort by a strong stimulus – a loud noise, bright light, sudden movement
  • Habitual attention – developed through habit and training – a mother waking at her baby's cry, a nurse alert to a monitor alarm

2. According to process

  • Selective attention – focusing on one message among many (hearing one's own name in a noisy room – the "cocktail party effect")
  • Sustained attention (vigilance) – keeping attention on a task for a long time (watching a cardiac monitor)
  • Divided attention – attending to two tasks at once; possible only when one task is automatic
  • Shifting (alternating) attention – moving focus from one task to another

B. Characteristics of attention

  1. Selectivity – attention has a limited capacity, so it selects
  2. Span of attention – the number of objects that can be grasped at a single glance is limited (about six to eight in adults); children have a shorter span than adults
  3. Fluctuation – attention wavers even on a constant stimulus (the ticking of a clock seems to come and go)
  4. Shifting – attention moves constantly from one object to another
  5. Division – true division is difficult; performance falls when two demanding tasks are done together
  6. Distraction – irrelevant stimuli interfere with attention; strong motivation reduces their effect

C. Alterations of attention

  • Distractibility – in mania and anxiety
  • Inattention – in attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and delirium (a core feature)
  • Poor concentration – in depression, fatigue, pain, hunger and intoxication

D. Importance in nursing

  • Nurse's own attention and patient safety:
    • avoid interruptions during medication rounds (some hospitals use "do not disturb" signs)
    • double-check high-risk drugs; respond to alarms
    • fatigue and long shifts reduce vigilance – adequate rest is important
  • Patient teaching:
    • teach when the patient is comfortable and free from pain
    • keep sessions short, use demonstrations and audio-visual aids, reduce noise
  • Distraction as a pain-relief method – music, television, stories and play for children
  • Assessment – attention is tested in the mental status examination (e.g. counting backwards, repeating digits)

Conclusion Attention is the selective focusing of consciousness; it may be voluntary, involuntary or habitual and has a limited span, fluctuates and can be distracted. Good attention is essential for patient safety and effective patient teaching.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain aptitude – its meaning, characteristics, types and measurement.
answer_html:
Introduction Aptitude is a person's natural capacity or potential to acquire a particular skill or knowledge with training. Bingham described it as a set of characteristics that indicates a person's ability to acquire, with training, some knowledge, skill or set of responses.

  • Aptitude – what a person can learn (potential)
  • Achievement – what he has already learned
  • Intelligence – general mental ability; aptitude is specific

A. Characteristics

  1. Specific – a person may have high musical aptitude but low mechanical aptitude
  2. Predictive – indicates future success in a field
  3. Partly inborn, developed by training and environment
  4. Individual differences – people differ widely in aptitudes
  5. Relatively stable after adolescence
  6. Related to, but different from, interest – a person may like a subject without having aptitude for it

B. Types of aptitude

  • Mechanical – understanding machines and tools
  • Clerical – speed and accuracy in office work
  • Verbal (language) and numerical
  • Spatial – visualising shapes and space
  • Artistic and musical
  • Scientific, teaching, medical and nursing aptitude

C. Measurement – aptitude tests

  • Differential Aptitude Test (DAT) – measures verbal reasoning, numerical ability, abstract reasoning, clerical speed and accuracy, mechanical reasoning, space relations and language usage; Indian adaptations are available
  • General Aptitude Test Battery (GATB)
  • Special aptitude tests – mechanical comprehension, clerical, musical and art judgement tests
  • Entrance and selection tests for courses and jobs partly measure aptitude

D. Uses

  1. Educational and vocational guidance – choosing the right course and career
  2. Selection of candidates for training and jobs (nursing, armed forces, pilots)
  3. Placement and promotion at work
  4. Counselling and self-understanding

E. Aptitude for nursing

  • Genuine interest in people and a caring attitude
  • Empathy, patience and emotional stability
  • Observation skills, accuracy and quick decision-making
  • Good communication and teamwork
  • Manual dexterity and physical stamina
  • Ability to work under stress and follow ethical rules

F. Aptitude, achievement and interest compared

Aptitude Achievement Interest
potential to learn a skill skill or knowledge already learned liking for an activity
looks to the future measures the past shows preference
e.g. aptitude test before admission e.g. end-of-year examination e.g. interest inventory

Conclusion Aptitude is a specific potential to learn a skill; it is partly inborn and developed by training, and is measured by tests such as the DAT. Aptitude testing helps in guidance and selection – including identifying people suited to nursing.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the alterations in cognitive processes.
answer_html:
Introduction Cognitive processes – attention, perception, memory, thinking, intelligence, orientation and judgement – can be altered by physical illness, brain disease, mental illness, drugs and ageing. Recognising these alterations helps in early diagnosis and safe nursing care.

1. Alterations of attention

  • Distractibility – mania, anxiety
  • Inattention – ADHD, delirium
  • Poor concentration – depression, fatigue, pain

2. Alterations of perception

  • Illusion – misinterpretation of a real stimulus (a rope seen as a snake); common in delirium and dim light
  • Hallucination – perception without any stimulus; auditory hallucinations are common in schizophrenia; visual hallucinations in delirium and alcohol withdrawal
  • Depersonalisation (feeling unreal) and derealisation (surroundings seem unreal)
  • Agnosia – inability to recognise objects despite normal senses (brain damage)

3. Alterations of memory

  • Amnesia – loss of memory; anterograde (cannot form new memories) or retrograde (loss of past memories), e.g. after head injury
  • Dementia – progressive loss of memory, recent memory first
  • Confabulation – filling memory gaps with made-up stories (Korsakoff's psychosis)
  • Déjà vu – a feeling that a new experience has happened before

4. Alterations of thinking

  • Form and flow of thought:
    • flight of ideas – rapid jumping from topic to topic (mania)
    • retardation – slow thinking (depression)
    • thought block, loosening of associations (schizophrenia)
    • perseveration – repeating the same idea
  • Content of thought:
    • delusion – a false, fixed belief not shared by the person's culture – of persecution, grandeur, guilt, jealousy
    • obsessions – unwanted, repeated thoughts (obsessive-compulsive disorder)
    • phobias – irrational fears

5. Alterations of intelligence

  • Intellectual disability – IQ below about 70 with limited adaptive skills, beginning in childhood
  • Dementia – loss of previously acquired intelligence

6. Alterations of orientation and consciousness

  • Disorientation to time, place and person – delirium, dementia
  • Clouding of consciousness, confusion, stupor and coma

7. Alterations of judgement and insight

  • Poor judgement – mania, dementia, intoxication
  • Lack of insight (not knowing one is ill) – psychosis

8. Common causes

  • Head injury, stroke, brain tumours; infections (meningitis, encephalitis)
  • Metabolic disorders – low blood sugar, liver or kidney failure, low oxygen
  • Alcohol and drugs; mental disorders; sleep and sensory deprivation; ageing

9. Role of the nurse

  • Assess orientation, attention, memory and level of consciousness (e.g. MMSE, Glasgow Coma Scale)
  • Safety – supervision, bed rails, fall prevention
  • Reorientation – clock, calendar, familiar objects, good lighting (reduces illusions)
  • Simple, clear communication; a fixed routine
  • Do not argue with delusions; do not support them either
  • Report sudden changes – delirium is a medical emergency
  • Support and educate the family

Conclusion Cognitive alterations include problems of attention, perception (illusions, hallucinations), memory (amnesia, confabulation), thinking (delusions, flight of ideas), intelligence, orientation and judgement; the nurse identifies them early, keeps the patient safe and supports recovery.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the motivation cycle.
answer_html:
Introduction The motivation cycle shows how a need leads to behaviour and how satisfaction of that need ends the behaviour, until a new need arises.

Stages of the motivation cycle

  1. Need – a lack or deficiency in the body or mind (lack of food)
  2. Drive – the state of tension or arousal produced by the need (hunger)
  3. Goal-directed behaviour – activity aimed at satisfying the need (looking for food)
  4. Goal (incentive) – the object that satisfies the need (food)
  5. Satisfaction (relief) – the need is met and tension is reduced
  6. New need – after some time the cycle starts again

subject: Applied Psychology
question: List the physiological changes during emotion.
answer_html:
Introduction During strong emotions such as fear and anger, the sympathetic nervous system and the adrenal medulla (adrenaline) prepare the body for "fight or flight".

Physiological changes

  1. Increased heart rate and blood pressure
  2. Rapid, deep breathing
  3. Dilated pupils
  4. Sweating, dry mouth, goose flesh
  5. Raised blood sugar – more energy
  6. Blood diverted from the gut and skin to the muscles and brain – pale skin, digestion slows
  7. Muscle tension, trembling
  8. Changes in voice and facial expression
  9. Frequency of urination or diarrhoea in some persons

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define attitude. Mention its components.
answer_html:
Definition An attitude is a learnt, relatively stable tendency to respond favourably or unfavourably towards a person, object, group or idea.

Components (ABC model)

  1. Affective – feelings or emotions ("I dislike injections")
  2. Behavioural – the tendency to act ("I avoid going to the hospital")
  3. Cognitive – beliefs and thoughts ("Injections are harmful")

Features: attitudes are learnt, can be positive or negative, vary in strength, are fairly stable, but can be changed through education and experience.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Describe the biological and social motives.
answer_html:
Introduction A motive is an inner force that arouses and directs behaviour towards a goal. Motives are broadly divided into biological (primary) motives, which are inborn and necessary for survival, and social (secondary) motives, which are learnt through interaction with society.

A. Biological (primary, physiological) motives These are unlearnt, common to all human beings and based on bodily needs. They work on the principle of homeostasis – keeping the internal environment balanced.

1. Hunger – produced by low blood sugar, stomach contractions and signals to the hypothalamus 2. Thirst – due to loss of body water and increased concentration of blood 3. Need for oxygen – the most urgent need; lack of air causes immediate distress 4. Sleep and rest – after fatigue 5. Temperature regulation – seeking warmth in cold and coolness in heat 6. Avoidance of pain – pulling away from harmful stimuli 7. Elimination – urination and defecation 8. Sex motive – necessary for continuation of the species; influenced by hormones and culture 9. Maternal motive – care and protection of the young

B. Social (secondary, learnt) motives These are acquired through family, culture and society. They vary from person to person.

1. Achievement motive – the desire to succeed and excel (David McClelland); a student working hard to top the class 2. Affiliation motive – the need to be with others, to make friends and to belong to a group 3. Power motive – the desire to influence and control others 4. Approval and recognition – wanting praise and respect 5. Curiosity and exploration – the need to know and discover new things 6. Security – the desire for a stable job, savings and a safe home 7. Aggression – a learnt tendency to attack when frustrated

C. Other classifications

  • Intrinsic motives – coming from within (enjoying nursing care itself)
  • Extrinsic motives – coming from outside rewards (salary, grades, prizes)
  • Conscious and unconscious motives (Freud)
  • Personal motives – habits, interests, attitudes, goals and level of aspiration

Nursing importance

  • In illness, biological needs come first – oxygen, fluids, food, rest and pain relief
  • Patients are motivated to follow treatment when their social needs – respect, recognition and belonging – are also met
  • Nurses use praise and recognition to motivate patients and students

Conclusion Biological motives arise from body needs and keep us alive, while social motives are learnt and give direction to life; nurses must meet both to motivate patients towards recovery.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Describe the factors affecting the formation of attitude and the methods of changing attitude.
answer_html:
Introduction An attitude is a learnt tendency to respond positively or negatively to a person, object or idea. It has affective (feeling), behavioural (action) and cognitive (belief) components. Attitudes towards health – smoking, vaccination, family planning, mental illness – strongly affect health behaviour.

A. Factors affecting the formation of attitude

1. Family

  • Children learn attitudes by imitating parents; e.g. a child of parents who fear hospitals develops the same fear

2. Peer group and friends

  • Especially in adolescence – attitudes towards smoking, dress and studies

3. Education

  • Schools and teachers shape attitudes towards hygiene, gender equality and science

4. Culture and religion

  • Beliefs about food, illness, birth, death and blood transfusion

5. Personal experience

  • A painful or pleasant experience in a hospital decides future attitude towards treatment

6. Mass media and social media

  • Television, films, advertisements and social media shape attitudes quickly

7. Needs, interests and personality

  • People develop favourable attitudes to things that satisfy their needs

B. Methods of changing attitude

1. Providing new information (education)

  • Health education with facts, demonstrations and examples

2. Persuasive communication

  • A credible, trusted source (a respected doctor or nurse) and a clear, repeated message are more effective

3. Personal contact and experience

  • Meeting a cured leprosy patient reduces fear and prejudice

4. Group discussion and group decision

  • People change more easily when the whole group agrees (mothers' meetings on breastfeeding)

5. Role models

  • Celebrities or local leaders promoting vaccination or blood donation

6. Role playing

  • Taking the role of another person increases understanding

7. Rewards and incentives

  • Incentives for institutional delivery or sterilisation

8. Creating cognitive dissonance (Festinger)

  • Showing a person that his belief and behaviour do not match ("You love your children, yet you smoke in front of them") creates discomfort that leads to change

9. Legal measures

  • Laws such as bans on smoking in public places and on dowry gradually change attitudes

C. Role of attitude in health and sickness

  • Positive attitudes lead to healthy practices and compliance with treatment; negative attitudes cause delay in seeking care and stigma (TB, HIV, mental illness)
  • The nurse's own attitude – respectful, non-judgemental and caring – builds patients' trust

Conclusion Attitudes are formed by family, peers, culture, experience and media, and can be changed by information, persuasion, contact, group decision and incentives; nurses use these methods in health education.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain emotions in sickness and the ways the nurse handles emotions in self and others.
answer_html:
Introduction An emotion is a strong feeling (such as fear, anger or joy) with physical changes (racing heart, sweating), expression (face, voice) and thoughts. Emotions develop from simple excitement in the newborn to complex emotions such as shame and pride in later childhood. Illness and hospitalisation produce strong emotions in patients and their families, and these emotions affect recovery.

A. Common emotions in sickness

  1. Fear and anxiety – of pain, injections, operation, diagnosis, cost of treatment, disability and death
  2. Anger – "Why me?"; anger at family, doctors or nurses
  3. Sadness and depression – loss of health, job, body part or independence
  4. Guilt – feeling the illness is a punishment or a burden on the family
  5. Shame and embarrassment – exposure during procedures, incontinence, disfigurement
  6. Helplessness and dependency
  7. Loneliness – separation from family and home
  8. Hope – a positive emotion that supports recovery

B. Effects on health

  • Anxiety increases pain, raises BP and pulse and delays wound healing
  • Depression causes poor appetite, poor sleep and non-compliance
  • Calmness and hope improve immunity and cooperation

C. Handling emotions in others (patients and relatives)

  • Accept the patient's feelings as real; do not say "Don't cry" or "Don't worry"
  • Listen actively and allow ventilation of feelings
  • Show empathy – "I understand this is frightening for you"
  • Give clear information and explain procedures – uncertainty increases fear
  • Maintain privacy and dignity
  • Use therapeutic touch, presence and a calm voice
  • Provide distraction – music, reading, prayer, visits
  • Teach relaxation – deep breathing and guided imagery
  • Respect spiritual and religious practices
  • Refer to the counsellor or psychiatrist when emotions are severe or prolonged

D. Handling emotions in self (the nurse)

  • Self-awareness – recognise one's own feelings such as grief when a patient dies, or anger at an abusive relative
  • Emotional intelligence – control impulses and respond professionally; do not displace anger on patients
  • Express feelings in healthy ways – talk with colleagues, debriefing after a stressful event
  • Adequate rest, hobbies, exercise, yoga and meditation
  • Maintain professional boundaries – be caring without over-involvement
  • Seek counselling when stress or grief persists

Conclusion Sickness brings fear, anger, sadness and dependency; a nurse who accepts, listens, informs and supports patients, and who manages her own emotions, promotes faster physical and emotional recovery.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define motivation. Explain the theories of motivation and the role of the nurse in caring for an emotionally sick client. (2 + 5 + 3)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • The word motivation comes from the Latin "movere", meaning to move
  • Motivation is the process that arouses, directs and sustains behaviour towards a goal
  • P. T. Young: motivation is "the process of arousing action, sustaining the activity in progress and regulating the pattern of activity"

Related terms

  • Need – a lack or deficiency (lack of water)
  • Drive – the tension produced by the need (thirst)
  • Incentive – the external goal that satisfies the need (water)
  • Motive – the inner force that directs behaviour

Types of motives: biological (hunger, thirst, sleep) and social (achievement, affiliation, power); intrinsic and extrinsic; conscious and unconscious.

Motivation cycle: need → drive → goal-directed behaviour → goal → satisfaction → new need.

(b) Theories of motivation (5 marks)

1. Instinct theory – William McDougall

  • Behaviour is driven by inborn instincts, each linked with an emotion – flight with fear, combat with anger, curiosity with wonder, parental instinct with tenderness
  • Limitation: it only names behaviour; it does not explain learnt behaviour

2. Drive-reduction theory – Clark Hull

  • A physiological need creates a drive (state of tension); behaviour aims to reduce the drive and restore homeostasis
  • Example: dehydration → thirst → drinking water → relief
  • Limitation: does not explain curiosity or thrill-seeking, which increase tension

3. Arousal theory and the Yerkes–Dodson law

  • People seek an optimum level of arousal
  • Performance is best at a moderate level of arousal; too little (boredom) or too much (panic) reduces performance
  • Example: mild exam tension helps a student study; severe anxiety blocks recall

4. Incentive theory

  • Behaviour is pulled by external rewards – money, praise, grades, prizes – rather than pushed by inner drives

5. Maslow's hierarchy of needs – Abraham Maslow (1943)

  • Human needs are arranged in a pyramid of five levels; lower needs must generally be met before higher needs motivate behaviour
    1. Physiological needs – oxygen, food, water, sleep, elimination, shelter
    2. Safety and security needs – protection from harm, stability, freedom from fear
    3. Love and belongingness needs – affection, family, friends, acceptance
    4. Esteem needs – self-respect, recognition, status
    5. Self-actualisation – becoming everything one is capable of becoming
  • The first four are deficiency needs; self-actualisation is a growth need
  • In nursing, it guides priority setting – airway, breathing and pain relief come before health teaching

6. Psychoanalytic theory – Sigmund Freud

  • Behaviour is driven by unconscious motives – the life instinct (Eros) and the death instinct (Thanatos)
  • Explains why people sometimes cannot explain their own behaviour

7. McClelland's need theory

  • Three learnt needs: need for achievement, need for affiliation and need for power

8. Herzberg's two-factor theory (at the workplace)

  • Hygiene factors – salary, working conditions, policies, supervision – prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate
  • Motivators – achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth and the work itself – produce real job satisfaction
  • Explains why recognition motivates nurses as much as pay

9. Expectancy theory – Victor Vroom

  • People are motivated when they expect that effort will lead to performance and that performance will bring a valued reward

Summary

Theory Psychologist Key idea
Instinct McDougall inborn instincts
Drive reduction Hull reduce body tension
Arousal Yerkes–Dodson moderate arousal is best
Hierarchy of needs Maslow five levels of needs
Psychoanalytic Freud unconscious motives
Need theory McClelland achievement, affiliation, power
Two-factor Herzberg hygiene factors and motivators

(c) Role of the nurse in caring for an emotionally sick client (3 marks) An emotionally sick client is one whose feelings – anxiety, sadness, anger, fear or hopelessness – are so intense that they disturb daily functioning.

1. Build a therapeutic relationship

  • Introduce yourself, be consistent, keep promises and maintain confidentiality to develop trust

2. Communicate therapeutically

  • Active listening, empathy and silence; allow ventilation of feelings
  • Accept the client without judging; avoid false reassurance and arguing

3. Ensure safety

  • Observe for suicidal ideas and aggression; remove sharp and harmful articles; close observation when needed

4. Meet basic needs first (Maslow)

  • Nutrition, fluids, hygiene, elimination and sleep

5. Provide a therapeutic environment
