  • Calm, quiet, well-lit surroundings with a structured daily routine

6. Help the client cope

  • Help identify feelings and their triggers
  • Teach relaxation (deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation), problem-solving and assertive expression of anger

7. Build self-esteem

  • Give small achievable tasks, praise progress, encourage self-care and decision-making

8. Encourage activity

  • Occupational therapy, recreation, group activities, prayer as per the client's beliefs

9. Medication and follow-up

  • Give prescribed drugs, observe effects and side effects, encourage compliance

10. Involve the family

  • Explain the illness, teach them to support the client and to recognise warning signs; arrange follow-up and referral to counsellors or psychiatrists

11. Self-awareness of the nurse

  • Remain calm and patient; do not take the client's anger personally

Conclusion Motivation is the force that arouses and directs behaviour. Theories from instincts and drives to Maslow's hierarchy and Herzberg's factors explain why people act. Using these ideas, the nurse meets the basic and emotional needs of an emotionally sick client through trust, safety, therapeutic communication and support.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define stress. Explain the types of stressors, the general adaptation syndrome, the effects of stress and the methods of coping. (2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2)

diagram.caption: Selye's general adaptation syndrome – alarm, resistance and exhaustion

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Hans Selye: "Stress is the non-specific response of the body to any demand made upon it"
  • In simple words, stress is the state of physical and mental tension that arises when a person feels that the demands on him are greater than his ability to cope
  • A stressor is any event or situation that produces stress
  • Eustress – positive stress that motivates (preparing for an exam, a wedding)
  • Distress – harmful stress that causes ill health
  • Stress cycle: stressor → appraisal ("Is this a threat?") → stress response → coping → adaptation or illness

(b) Types of stressors (2 marks)

  1. Physical – heat, cold, noise, injury, surgery, pain
  2. Chemical – drugs, poisons, alcohol, pollutants
  3. Biological – infections, illness, hormonal changes
  4. Psychological – fear, conflict, frustration, examinations, low self-esteem
  5. Social – death of a spouse, divorce, unemployment, poverty, family quarrels, migration
  6. Developmental – puberty, marriage, pregnancy, menopause, retirement
  7. Occupational – workload, night shifts, staff shortage, conflict with seniors
  8. Environmental – overcrowding, floods, earthquakes and other disasters

Life events: Holmes and Rahe's Social Readjustment Rating Scale gives the death of a spouse the highest score (100 units); a high total score in a year increases the chances of illness.

(c) General adaptation syndrome (GAS) (2 marks) Selye described the body's response to prolonged stress in three stages:

1. Alarm reaction

  • The body recognises the stressor and prepares for "fight or flight"
  • Activation of the sympathetic nervous system and the hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal axis; release of adrenaline and cortisol
  • Rise in pulse, BP, respiration and blood sugar; pupils dilate; resistance falls briefly (shock) and then rises (counter-shock)

2. Stage of resistance

  • The body tries to adapt to the stressor; hormone levels remain high
  • If the stressor is removed or the person copes, the body returns to normal

3. Stage of exhaustion

  • If stress continues for a long time, the body's energy is used up
  • Resistance breaks down – "diseases of adaptation" such as hypertension, peptic ulcer and depression; in extreme cases, death

Local adaptation syndrome (LAS): a response in one part of the body, such as inflammation at a wound or the reflex withdrawal of a hand from heat.

(d) Effects of stress (2 marks)

  • Physical – headache, palpitations, hypertension, heart disease, peptic ulcer, irritable bowel, asthma attacks, poor control of diabetes, menstrual irregularity, low immunity, insomnia, fatigue
  • Psychological – anxiety, irritability, depression, poor concentration, forgetfulness, burnout
  • Behavioural – smoking, alcohol and drug use, over-eating or loss of appetite, withdrawal, absenteeism, accidents, aggression
  • Positive effects – moderate stress (eustress) improves alertness, motivation and performance

(e) Methods of coping (2 marks) Coping is the effort a person makes to manage stress. Adaptation is the successful adjustment that results.

Types of coping

  • Problem-focused coping – acting on the cause (making a study timetable before exams)
  • Emotion-focused coping – managing the feelings (talking to a friend, praying)
  • Adaptive (healthy) coping – exercise, problem-solving, seeking help
  • Maladaptive (unhealthy) coping – alcohol, smoking, denial, withdrawal

Stress management techniques

  1. Identify stressors and remove or reduce them where possible
  2. Time management – plan, prioritise, avoid last-minute rush
  3. Relaxation – deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation (Jacobson), yoga, pranayama and meditation
  4. Regular exercise, adequate sleep and a balanced diet
  5. Social support – family, friends, support groups
  6. Positive thinking – changing negative thoughts ("I will fail") into realistic ones ("I have prepared well")
  7. Hobbies, music, humour and recreation
  8. Assertiveness – learning to say "no"
  9. Spiritual practices – prayer, faith
  10. Counselling when stress is severe; avoid alcohol and drugs

Nursing importance

  • Patients: reduce hospital stressors – explain procedures, relieve pain, maintain privacy, allow family visits, teach relaxation
  • Nurses: shift work and heavy workloads cause stress and burnout; nurses need time management, peer support and self-care

Conclusion Stress is the body's response to any demand. Stressors may be physical, psychological, social or developmental; prolonged stress passes through the alarm, resistance and exhaustion stages and causes illness. Healthy coping – relaxation, exercise, support and problem-solving – leads to adaptation.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: What is emotional maturity? List its characteristics.
answer_html:
Definition Emotional maturity is the ability to understand, control and express one's emotions appropriately for one's age and situation, and to respond sensibly to the emotions of others. It develops gradually through experience.

Characteristics of an emotionally mature person

  1. Controls emotions – no temper outbursts; expresses feelings in acceptable ways
  2. Tolerates frustration and can wait for rewards
  3. Accepts criticism and failure and learns from mistakes
  4. Takes responsibility for his actions; does not blame others
  5. Shows empathy and consideration for others
  6. Is emotionally independent
  7. Is realistic and flexible; adapts to change
  8. Has a stable mood and a sense of humour

Importance for nurses: helps them remain calm in emergencies and handle difficult patients and relatives.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Differentiate between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation.
answer_html:
Introduction Motivation is the inner force that starts, directs and maintains behaviour. It may come from within or from outside.

Intrinsic motivation Extrinsic motivation
comes from within the person comes from outside the person
activity done for its own sake – interest, enjoyment, satisfaction, curiosity done for an external reward or to avoid punishment
e.g. a nurse caring for patients because she finds it meaningful e.g. working for salary, promotion, marks, praise or fear of punishment
long-lasting; promotes creativity and deep learning may stop when the reward stops

Application: both are useful – praise and rewards (extrinsic) can build genuine interest (intrinsic); in patient teaching, explain the benefits and praise progress.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the theories of emotion.
answer_html:
Introduction An emotion is a complex state of feeling accompanied by physiological changes (fast heartbeat, sweating) and expressive behaviour (facial expression, crying). Theories of emotion try to explain the relationship between the bodily changes and the feeling.

1. Common-sense view

  • Stimulus → feeling → bodily changes
  • "We see a snake, feel afraid and then tremble"

2. James–Lange theory (William James and Carl Lange)

  • Stimulus → bodily changes → our awareness of these changes is the emotion
  • "We feel afraid because we tremble; we feel sad because we cry"
  • Criticism – the same bodily changes occur in different emotions; emotions are still felt when signals from the body are cut off; bodily changes are too slow to explain sudden emotions

3. Cannon–Bard theory (Walter Cannon and Philip Bard)

  • The stimulus reaches the thalamus, which sends signals at the same time to:
    • the cortex → the conscious feeling of emotion
    • the body (through the hypothalamus and autonomic nerves) → bodily changes
  • Feeling and bodily reaction occur simultaneously and independently
  • Criticism – the hypothalamus and limbic system play a bigger role than the thalamus

4. Schachter–Singer two-factor theory

  • Emotion = physiological arousal + a cognitive label (interpretation of the situation)
  • The same arousal (racing heart) may be felt as fear or excitement, depending on how we interpret the situation

5. Cognitive appraisal theory (Richard Lazarus)

  • Our appraisal (evaluation) of a situation comes first and decides the emotion and the bodily response
  • Explains why two people react differently to the same event – e.g. one patient is terrified of surgery, another is relieved

6. Facial feedback hypothesis

  • Facial expressions can strengthen the feeling – smiling may make us feel happier

Comparison at a glance

Theory Sequence
James–Lange stimulus → bodily change → emotion
Cannon–Bard stimulus → bodily change and emotion together
Schachter–Singer arousal + interpretation → emotion
Lazarus appraisal → emotion and bodily change

Application in nursing

  • A patient's interpretation of his illness shapes his emotions – the nurse explains, corrects misconceptions and reassures
  • Relaxation and slow breathing reduce bodily arousal and so reduce anxiety
  • A pleasant, smiling approach helps patients feel calmer

Conclusion James–Lange held that emotion follows bodily changes, Cannon–Bard that both occur together, Schachter–Singer that arousal plus interpretation produces emotion, and Lazarus that appraisal comes first; these ideas help nurses manage patients' fear and anxiety.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain emotional intelligence and its importance in nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Emotional intelligence (EI) is the ability to recognise, understand and manage one's own emotions, and to recognise and influence the emotions of others. The term was introduced by Peter Salovey and John Mayer (1990) and made popular by Daniel Goleman (1995), who argued that it can matter as much as IQ for success. It is measured as the emotional quotient (EQ).

A. Components (Goleman)

  1. Self-awareness – knowing one's own emotions, strengths and weaknesses; self-confidence
  2. Self-regulation – controlling impulses and moods; thinking before acting; adaptability
  3. Motivation – inner drive to achieve; optimism and commitment
  4. Empathy – understanding the feelings of others; sensitivity to patients' needs
  5. Social skills – communication, conflict management, teamwork, leadership and building rapport

Mayer–Salovey model: perceiving, using, understanding and managing emotions.

B. Importance in nursing

  1. Therapeutic nurse–patient relationship – empathy and understanding increase patient satisfaction and cooperation
  2. Handling stressful situations – emergencies, deaths, aggressive relatives – calmly
  3. Prevents burnout and improves job satisfaction and resilience
  4. Communication and teamwork – fewer conflicts, better cooperation
  5. Leadership – ward in-charges with high EI motivate their teams
  6. Clinical decisions – emotions do not cloud judgement
  7. Patient safety – calm, focused nurses make fewer errors
  8. Sensitive situations – breaking bad news, end-of-life care, caring for anxious children and parents

C. Developing emotional intelligence

  • Self-reflection and keeping a reflective diary
  • Asking for and accepting feedback
  • Mindfulness, meditation and yoga
  • Practising active listening and empathy
  • Recognising one's emotional triggers and pausing before reacting
  • Role-plays and communication training

D. Emotional intelligence and IQ compared

Emotional intelligence (EQ) Intelligence (IQ)
ability to understand and manage emotions ability to reason, learn and solve problems
can be developed throughout life relatively stable
predicts success in relationships, teamwork and leadership predicts academic performance

E. Signs of low emotional intelligence in a nurse

  • Frequent arguments with colleagues and patients
  • Taking feedback as a personal attack
  • Inability to stay calm in emergencies
  • Little attention to how patients feel

Conclusion Emotional intelligence – self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills – enables nurses to build therapeutic relationships, work well in teams, cope with stress and give safe, compassionate care; it can be developed through reflection and practice.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain adjustment and the causes of maladjustment.
answer_html:
Introduction Adjustment is the process by which a person tries to satisfy his needs and cope with the demands of the environment, achieving harmony between himself and his surroundings. Shaffer described it as the process by which a person maintains a balance between his needs and the circumstances that affect their satisfaction. Adaptation usually refers to biological adjustment.

A. Process of adjustment

  • Need or motive → obstacle → frustration or conflict → varied responses (trial and error) → solution → adjustment
  • If no solution is found → maladjustment

B. Characteristics of a well-adjusted person

  • Realistic view of self and the world
  • Accepts himself and others
  • Emotional balance and satisfaction of needs
  • Good relationships; efficient at work
  • Flexible and able to cope with stress
  • Behaviour acceptable to society

C. Methods of adjustment

  • Direct (task-oriented) – more effort, changing or substituting the goal, problem-solving, compromise, seeking help
  • Indirect – healthy, occasional use of defence mechanisms

D. Maladjustment Maladjustment is the failure to adjust – behaviour becomes harmful to the person or others and causes distress.

Signs

  • Anxiety, irritability, aggression or withdrawal
  • Poor performance at school or work
  • Substance use, physical complaints without a physical cause, delinquency

Causes

  1. Personal – physical illness or disability, low intelligence, poor self-concept, emotional immaturity, unrealistic goals
  2. Family – broken homes, rejection, overprotection, inconsistent discipline, favouritism, sibling rivalry
  3. School and work – academic failure, unsuitable course or job, harsh teachers or supervisors, heavy workload
  4. Social – poverty, discrimination, rejection by peers, cultural conflict, migration
  5. Unresolved frustration and conflict; excessive stress; over-use of defence mechanisms

E. Role of the nurse

  • Identify signs of maladjustment in patients, students and colleagues
  • Counsel and help set realistic goals; teach coping and problem-solving skills
  • Strengthen support systems – family, friends, groups
  • Help patients adjust to illness, hospitalisation and disability through orientation, information and rehabilitation
  • Refer to counsellors or mental health services when needed

F. Adjustment and adaptation compared

  • Adaptation – mainly biological change to suit the environment (e.g. sweating in heat, more red cells at high altitude)
  • Adjustment – mainly psychological and social change to satisfy needs and get along with others (e.g. a new nursing student learning hostel rules and making friends)

Conclusion Adjustment is the continuous process of balancing one's needs with the demands of the environment; maladjustment results from personal, family, school, work and social factors, and nurses help people adjust through counselling, support and teaching coping skills.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: List the characteristics of a good psychological test.
answer_html:
Introduction A psychological test is an objective and standardised measure of a sample of behaviour.

Characteristics of a good test

  1. Standardisation – same instructions, conditions and scoring for everyone
  2. Objectivity – the score does not depend on the examiner's opinion
  3. Reliability – gives consistent results when repeated
  4. Validity – measures what it is meant to measure
  5. Norms – average scores of a reference group for comparison
  6. Practicability – easy to give, score and interpret; economical
  7. Discriminating power – separates high and low scorers
  8. Comprehensiveness – covers the whole area being tested

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define reliability and validity of a psychological test.
answer_html:
Reliability

  • Reliability is the consistency of a test – it gives the same results when repeated on the same persons under similar conditions
  • Methods: test–retest, parallel (alternate) forms, split-half and inter-rater reliability

Validity

  • Validity is the extent to which a test measures what it claims to measure
  • Types: content validity, criterion validity (concurrent and predictive), construct validity and face validity

Example: a weighing machine that always shows 2 kg extra is reliable (consistent) but not valid (not accurate). A test must be reliable to be valid, but a reliable test is not always valid.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Classify psychological tests.
answer_html:
Introduction A psychological test is an objective and standardised measure of a sample of behaviour (Anne Anastasi). Tests are used to measure abilities, personality, interests and attitudes. They can be classified in several ways.

1. According to what they measure (purpose)

  • Intelligence tests – Stanford–Binet, Wechsler scales, Bhatia's Battery, Raven's Progressive Matrices
  • Aptitude tests – measure potential to learn a skill; e.g. the Differential Aptitude Test (DAT), nursing aptitude tests
  • Achievement tests – measure what has been learnt; e.g. university examinations
  • Personality tests – MMPI, 16 PF, Rorschach, TAT
  • Interest inventories – Strong Interest Inventory, Kuder Preference Record
  • Attitude scales – Likert and Thurstone scales
  • Neuropsychological tests – Bender Visual Motor Gestalt test, memory scales
  • Clinical rating scales – depression and anxiety scales, Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE)

2. According to administration

  • Individual tests – one person at a time; detailed, but time-consuming (Wechsler scales)
  • Group tests – many persons at a time; economical (Army Alpha, entrance tests)

3. According to the material used

  • Verbal (paper–pencil) tests – need language and reading
  • Non-verbal and performance tests – use pictures, blocks, form boards; useful for children, illiterate persons and those with speech problems

4. According to time

  • Speed tests – many easy items in a fixed short time
  • Power tests – items of increasing difficulty with enough time

5. According to scoring

  • Objective tests – fixed answers, same score by any examiner (MCQs, inventories)
  • Subjective tests – scoring depends on the examiner's judgement (essays, projective tests)

6. According to construction

  • Standardised tests – prepared by experts with norms, reliability and validity
  • Teacher-made (non-standardised) tests – class tests

7. According to interpretation

  • Norm-referenced – compares a person with others (percentile, IQ)
  • Criterion-referenced – compares performance with a fixed standard (passing marks)

8. According to structure

  • Structured tests – clear questions and fixed responses (inventories)
  • Unstructured (projective) tests – ambiguous stimuli (inkblots, pictures)

Summary table

Basis Types
Purpose intelligence, aptitude, achievement, personality, interest, attitude
Administration individual, group
Material verbal, non-verbal / performance
Time speed, power
Scoring objective, subjective
Interpretation norm-referenced, criterion-referenced

Nursing importance

  • Nurses commonly use rating scales (MMSE, depression and pain scales) and assist psychologists with other tests

Conclusion Psychological tests are classified by purpose, administration, material, time, scoring, construction and interpretation; knowing these types helps nurses understand test reports and assist in assessment.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the role of the nurse in psychological assessment.
answer_html:
Introduction Psychological assessment is the systematic collection and interpretation of information about a person's thinking, feelings, behaviour and abilities, using interviews, observation and tests. Nurses spend the most time with patients, so their observations and support are a vital part of assessment.

1. Before the assessment

  • Explain the purpose of the test to the patient and family in simple words and obtain informed consent
  • Reduce anxiety – reassure that it is not a "pass or fail" examination
  • Ensure the patient is rested, fed and comfortable; check that he has used the toilet
  • Make sure spectacles and hearing aids are available
  • Note any drugs that may affect performance (sedatives)
  • Arrange a quiet, well-lit, distraction-free room

2. During the assessment

  • Assist the psychologist as needed
  • Observe the patient's behaviour – cooperation, attention, anxiety, speech and mood
  • Do not prompt or help the patient with answers

3. Collecting information

  • Take a nursing history – personal, family, developmental, social and medical
  • Collect collateral information from the family
  • Record ward behaviour – sleep, appetite, interaction, self-care, mood swings and unusual behaviour – which is valuable data for diagnosis

4. Administering simple scales

  • Trained nurses use screening tools such as the Mini-Mental State Examination, depression screening questionnaires, anxiety scales, suicide risk assessment and pain scales

5. After the assessment

  • Record and report observations accurately and objectively
  • Maintain confidentiality of results; share only with the treating team
  • Use the results to plan individualised nursing care – e.g. simple instructions for a patient with low IQ or memory impairment
  • Re-assess at intervals to monitor progress and the effect of treatment

6. Education and support

  • Explain the results (as advised by the team) to the family without labelling the patient
  • Support the patient emotionally if the results are upsetting

7. Ethical responsibilities

  • Respect the patient's rights and dignity; avoid misuse of test results; tests only by qualified persons

Conclusion The nurse prepares the patient and environment, observes behaviour, collects history, uses simple screening scales, records findings and uses the results to plan care, while protecting the patient's rights and confidentiality.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define a psychological test. Explain the steps in the development of a psychological test, the principles of administration and interpretation, and the uses of psychological tests. (2 + 3 + 3 + 2)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Anne Anastasi: "A psychological test is essentially an objective and standardised measure of a sample of behaviour"
  • Cronbach: "A test is a systematic procedure for comparing the behaviour of two or more persons"
  • In simple words, a psychological test is a standard tool for measuring abilities, personality, interests or attitudes so that a person can be compared with others or with a standard

Characteristics: standardisation, objectivity, reliability, validity, norms, practicability and discriminating power.

(b) Steps in the development of a psychological test (3 marks)

1. Planning

  • Decide the purpose (what to measure), the target group (age, education), the content areas and the type of items (MCQ, true/false, performance tasks), the time limit and the method of scoring

2. Writing the items (item pool)

  • Prepare more items than needed; items must be clear, simple, free from ambiguity and culturally suitable

3. Preliminary try-out (pilot study)

  • Give the draft test to a small sample similar to the target group; note unclear items, time taken and difficulties

4. Item analysis

  • Difficulty index – the percentage of persons answering an item correctly; very easy and very hard items are removed
  • Discrimination index – how well the item separates high scorers from low scorers

5. Final selection and arrangement of items

  • Good items are selected and arranged, usually from easy to difficult

6. Establishing reliability

  • By test–retest, split-half or parallel-forms methods

7. Establishing validity

  • Content, criterion (concurrent and predictive) and construct validity

8. Standardisation and norms

  • The test is given to a large representative sample; norms (age norms, grade norms, percentiles, standard scores) are prepared

9. Preparing the manual

  • A manual containing instructions for administration, scoring keys, norms, reliability, validity and interpretation

(c) Principles of administration and interpretation (3 marks)

Principles of administration

  1. Tests should be given only by trained and qualified persons
  2. Obtain informed consent and explain the purpose
  3. Provide a suitable environment – quiet, well-lit, ventilated, free from interruptions
  4. Establish rapport – make the person comfortable and cooperative
  5. Check the person's physical state – fatigue, illness, hunger, drugs, need for spectacles or hearing aids
  6. Follow the standard instructions exactly as given in the manual
  7. Maintain exact timing for timed tests
  8. Do not help, hint or coach
  9. Score accurately using the scoring key
  10. Maintain confidentiality of results

Principles of interpretation

  1. Convert raw scores into standard scores and compare them with the appropriate norms (same age, education and culture)
  2. Consider the person's background – language, education, culture, socio-economic status and health
  3. Never base a decision on a single test; combine with interview, history and observation
  4. Remember that every score has some error of measurement
  5. Report results in simple, non-labelling language and focus on strengths as well as weaknesses
  6. Interpret within the limits of the test – a test of memory does not measure personality

(d) Uses of psychological tests (2 marks)

  • Clinical diagnosis – intellectual disability, dementia, depression, personality disorders
  • Planning treatment and evaluating progress after therapy
  • Educational guidance – identifying gifted children, slow learners and learning disabilities
  • Vocational guidance and selection – choosing suitable courses and careers; selection of employees
  • Counselling of students and clients
  • Research in psychology, education and nursing
  • Forensic use – assessing a person's mental competence in legal cases

Common tests used in clinical settings

Test Measures
Mini-Mental State Examination (score out of 30) cognitive function, dementia
Wechsler scales, Bhatia's Battery intelligence
Vineland Social Maturity Scale social maturity (social quotient)
Beck Depression Inventory, Hamilton scales depression, anxiety
Bender Visual Motor Gestalt test brain damage, visual-motor function
MMPI, Rorschach, TAT personality

Role of the nurse (in brief)

  • Prepare the patient and environment, observe behaviour, assist the psychologist, use simple screening scales, maintain confidentiality and use results in care planning

Conclusion A psychological test is an objective, standardised measure of a sample of behaviour. It is developed through planning, item writing, try-out, item analysis, reliability, validity and norms; it must be administered and interpreted by set principles; and it is widely used in diagnosis, guidance, selection, treatment and research.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: What is a rating scale? Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition A rating scale is a tool on which an observer (or the person himself) records the degree or intensity of a trait, behaviour, symptom or attitude on a graded scale of numbers or descriptions.

Types

  1. Numerical – e.g. 0 to 10
  2. Graphic – a line or pictures
  3. Descriptive – poor, fair, good, excellent
  4. Likert scale – strongly agree to strongly disagree (attitude measurement)

Examples in health care

  • Numerical pain rating scale; Wong–Baker FACES scale for children
  • Glasgow Coma Scale; Apgar score
  • Braden scale (pressure ulcer risk)
  • Depression rating scales (Hamilton, Beck)
  • Clinical evaluation of nursing students

Limitations: halo effect, central tendency (rating everyone as average), leniency and personal bias.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE).
answer_html:
Introduction The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), developed by Folstein and colleagues (1975), is a brief 30-point questionnaire used to screen for cognitive impairment – as in dementia and delirium – and to follow changes over time. It takes about 5–10 minutes.

A. Areas tested and scores

Area What is tested Points
Orientation year, season, date, day, month; country, state, district or town, hospital, floor 10
Registration repeat three unrelated words (e.g. apple, table, coin) 3
Attention and calculation subtract 7 from 100 serially (93, 86, 79, 72, 65) or spell a word backwards 5
Recall recall the three words 3
Language and praxis name two objects, repeat a phrase, follow a three-stage command, read and obey "Close your eyes", write a sentence, copy two overlapping pentagons 9
Total 30

B. Interpretation (commonly used)

  • 24–30 – usually normal
  • 18–23 – mild cognitive impairment
  • Below 18 – severe impairment
  • Scores must be judged against the person's age and education; illiterate people may score low without dementia – the Hindi Mental State Examination (HMSE) was adapted for such rural populations

C. Uses

  • Screening for dementia and delirium
  • Monitoring the progress of dementia
  • Baseline assessment of elderly patients before surgery
  • Assessment after head injury or stroke; research

D. Limitations

  • Affected by education, language, culture, poor vision or hearing, and depression
  • Not a diagnosis by itself – only a screening tool
  • Less sensitive to very mild impairment; other tools such as the MoCA and Mini-Cog are also used

E. Role of the nurse

  • Choose a quiet, well-lit place; ensure the patient wears spectacles and hearing aids
  • Explain the purpose; put the patient at ease
  • Follow the standard instructions exactly; do not help or give hints
  • Record the exact score, date and any difficulties
  • Compare with earlier scores; report a decline promptly
  • Use the patient's own language

F. Example of recording

  • "MMSE 21/30 – lost points mainly in recall and attention; score was 26/30 three months ago. Patient wore spectacles; tested in Marathi. Reported to the doctor."
  • Such clear recording allows changes to be compared over time

Conclusion The MMSE is a quick 30-point screening test of orientation, registration, attention, recall and language; interpreted with regard to age and education, it helps nurses and doctors detect and monitor cognitive impairment.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: List the barriers to interpersonal relationship.
answer_html:
Introduction An interpersonal relationship (IPR) is a close association between two or more persons. Certain factors block the development of a good relationship.

Barriers to IPR

  1. Poor communication – unclear messages, medical jargon, language differences
  2. Poor listening – interrupting, not paying attention
  3. Prejudice and stereotypes – judging a person by caste, religion, gender or illness
  4. Lack of trust – broken promises, breach of confidentiality
  5. Emotional barriers – anger, anxiety, fear, low self-esteem
  6. Ego and negative attitudes – superiority, rudeness, lack of empathy
  7. Cultural differences in values, customs and gender norms
  8. Status and hierarchy differences
  9. Physical barriers – noise, distance, hearing or speech problems
  10. Lack of time and heavy workload

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Enumerate the uses of soft skills in nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Soft skills are personal and interpersonal skills – communication, empathy, teamwork, time management – that help a person work well with others.

Uses in nursing

  1. Therapeutic communication and building trust with patients
  2. Effective patient and family education
  3. Showing empathy and compassion, which improves patient satisfaction
  4. Teamwork with doctors, colleagues and other health workers
  5. Clear handover and reporting, which reduces errors
  6. Conflict resolution with patients, relatives and staff
  7. Time management and prioritising care
  8. Leadership and decision-making in the ward
  9. Cultural sensitivity while caring for diverse patients
  10. Coping with stress and preventing burnout

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define resilience. Mention ways to build it.
answer_html:
Definition Resilience is the ability to bounce back from stress, difficulties, failure or trauma and to adapt positively. A resilient person bends under pressure but does not break.

Ways to build resilience

  1. Maintain supportive relationships – family, friends, mentors
  2. Develop a positive, realistic outlook and hope
  3. Accept change as part of life
  4. Use problem-solving instead of avoiding problems
  5. Take care of health – sleep, exercise, diet, relaxation
  6. Learn from past experiences and failures
  7. Keep a sense of purpose and humour

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Differentiate between soft skills and hard skills.
answer_html:
Introduction A good nurse needs two kinds of skills. Hard skills are the technical knowledge and procedures needed to do the job. Soft skills are the personal, social and communication abilities that decide how well a person works with others. Hard skills may get a nurse the job, but soft skills decide how well she does it.

Definitions

  • Hard skills – specific, teachable and measurable technical abilities (e.g. catheterisation, drug calculation)
  • Soft skills – personal attributes and interpersonal abilities that help a person interact effectively and harmoniously with others (e.g. empathy, communication, teamwork)

Differences

Point Hard skills Soft skills
Nature technical, job-specific personal, interpersonal, behavioural
Based on knowledge and practice of procedures personality, attitudes, emotional intelligence
Brain mainly "IQ" – logical, analytical mainly "EQ" – emotional, social
How learnt classroom teaching, laboratory, training, practice experience, observation, self-awareness, role models, feedback
Measurement easy to test and certify (practical exams, OSCE) difficult to measure; observed in behaviour
Transferability specific to a job or field useful in every job and in personal life
Rules follow fixed rules and steps depend on the situation and the person
Examples (nursing) IV cannulation, injection, dressing, catheterisation, ECG recording, CPR, drug calculation, use of ventilator communication, listening, empathy, teamwork, leadership, time management, problem-solving, conflict management, adaptability
Change over time need updating as technology changes improve with experience and maturity

Why both are needed

  • A nurse who gives a perfect injection but is rude will lose the patient's trust; a kind nurse without technical skill can harm the patient
  • Example: before inserting a urinary catheter (hard skill), the nurse explains the procedure, ensures privacy and reassures the patient (soft skills)
  • Patient safety, satisfaction and good outcomes need competence plus compassion

How to develop soft skills

  • Practise active listening, observe good role models, ask for feedback, role play, participate in group work and develop self-awareness

Conclusion Hard skills are technical, measurable abilities, while soft skills are personal and interpersonal qualities; a competent nurse combines both to give safe, caring and effective nursing care.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the techniques of time management for nurses.
answer_html:
Introduction Time management is the process of planning and controlling how much time is spent on specific activities so that work is done efficiently and on time. In a busy ward, with many patients, procedures, documentation and emergencies, good time management makes the difference between safe care and chaos.

Importance

  • Completes work on time and reduces stress
  • Improves quality and safety of patient care
  • Leaves time for rest, family and personal growth (work–life balance)

Techniques of time management

1. Planning

  • Plan the day or shift in advance – review patients, medicines and procedures at handover
  • Prepare a to-do list and a daily or weekly timetable

2. Setting goals

  • Use SMART goals – Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-bound

3. Prioritising

  • ABC priority – A: must be done now; B: should be done today; C: can be done later
  • Urgent–important matrix (Eisenhower): do urgent and important tasks first (a patient in respiratory distress); schedule important but not urgent tasks (care plans, teaching); delegate urgent but less important tasks; drop tasks that are neither
  • In clinical care, use ABC (airway, breathing, circulation) and Maslow's hierarchy to set priorities

4. Scheduling and clustering

  • Group activities for the same patient – vital signs, medication and dressing in one visit
  • Schedule routine work at fixed times

5. Delegation

  • Assign suitable tasks to junior staff and attendants with clear instructions and supervision

6. Avoiding time wasters

  • Unnecessary chatting, personal phone use, unplanned meetings, frequent interruptions, searching for misplaced equipment, procrastination and perfectionism

7. Organising the workplace

  • Keep trolleys, trays and stores ready and arranged; restock at the end of each shift

8. Learning to say "no" politely to non-essential demands

9. Using technology

  • Reminders, alarms, electronic records and checklists

10. Taking breaks and evaluating

  • Short breaks maintain efficiency; at the end of the day, review what worked and what needs change

Conclusion Planning, goal setting, prioritising, clustering activities, delegation and avoiding time wasters help nurses complete work efficiently, reduce stress and give safe, timely care.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain resilience and work–life balance as survival strategies for nurses.
answer_html:
Introduction Nursing is rewarding but stressful – long shifts, night duties, emotional situations, heavy workload and family responsibilities. Survival strategies such as resilience and work–life balance help nurses stay healthy, avoid burnout and continue giving good care.

A. Resilience

1. Meaning

  • The ability to recover quickly from difficulties and adapt positively to stress, failure or trauma

2. Characteristics of a resilient person

  • Realistic optimism and hope
  • Emotional control and self-awareness
  • Good problem-solving skills
  • Flexibility – accepts change
  • Strong social support
  • Sense of purpose and humour

3. Building resilience in nurses

  • Build supportive relationships with colleagues and mentors
  • Use debriefing after difficult events such as a patient's death or a violent incident
  • Practise positive self-talk and learn from mistakes instead of blaming oneself
  • Develop clinical competence, which increases confidence
  • Care for the body – sleep, nutrition, exercise; practise yoga and meditation
  • Keep a spiritual or meaningful focus – remember why one chose nursing

B. Work–life balance

1. Meaning

  • A state in which a person gives adequate time and energy to both work and personal life – family, health, leisure and self-development

2. Signs of imbalance

  • Constant tiredness, irritability, poor sleep, frequent illness, family conflicts, no time for oneself, loss of interest in work

3. Strategies for work–life balance

  • Plan shifts and duties in advance; use leave wisely
  • Set boundaries – avoid carrying work worries home
  • Use time management – prioritise and delegate
  • Make time for family, hobbies and recreation
  • Maintain a healthy lifestyle – regular meals even on night duty, exercise and sleep
  • Learn to say no to unnecessary commitments
  • Seek family support in sharing household work
  • Use organisational support – flexible rosters, crèche facilities, counselling services, adequate staffing

C. Importance for nurses

  • Prevents burnout and compassion fatigue
  • Improves job satisfaction and reduces absenteeism and turnover
  • Improves quality and safety of patient care
  • Protects the nurse's physical and mental health and family life

Conclusion Resilience helps nurses bounce back from stress, and work–life balance keeps work and personal life in harmony; together they are essential survival strategies for a healthy and long nursing career.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define interpersonal relationship. Explain the types and purposes of interpersonal relationship, the barriers to it and the strategies to overcome the barriers. (2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • An interpersonal relationship (IPR) is a strong, deep or close association between two or more people, based on feelings, mutual interest, regular interaction or social commitment
  • It involves communication, trust, respect and mutual understanding
  • In nursing, the nurse–patient relationship is a special, therapeutic interpersonal relationship aimed at helping the patient
  • Hildegard Peplau, in her theory of Interpersonal Relations in Nursing (1952), described nursing itself as a therapeutic interpersonal process

Interpersonal skills: communication, active listening, empathy, assertiveness, teamwork, negotiation, conflict resolution, problem-solving and decision-making.

(b) Types of interpersonal relationship (2 marks)

1. Personal relationships

  • Family – parents, children, siblings, spouse
  • Friendship – based on mutual liking and trust
  • Romantic or marital relationships

2. Professional relationships

  • Nurse–patient (therapeutic), nurse–doctor, nurse–colleague, teacher–student, supervisor–subordinate

3. Social relationships

  • Neighbours, community members, acquaintances

4. By formality

  • Formal – governed by rules and roles (nurse and hospital administrator)
  • Informal – casual and friendly (colleagues during lunch)

5. By duration

  • Short-term (a patient in day-care surgery) and long-term (a patient on dialysis for years)

Phases of the therapeutic nurse–patient relationship

  1. Pre-interaction phase – the nurse studies the patient's records and examines her own feelings
  2. Orientation (introductory) phase – introduction, building trust, explaining roles and confidentiality, forming a contract
  3. Working phase – exploring problems, giving care, teaching and helping the patient develop coping skills
  4. Termination phase – reviewing progress, preparing for discharge and ending the relationship smoothly

(Peplau described the phases as orientation, identification, exploitation and resolution.)

(c) Purposes of interpersonal relationship (2 marks)

  • To meet emotional and social needs – love, belonging and support
  • To build trust and cooperation between nurse and patient
  • To assess the patient's needs and problems accurately
  • To give therapeutic help – emotional support, counselling and patient teaching
  • To share information clearly among the health team
  • To promote teamwork and coordination
  • To give support in crisis – illness, loss, death
  • To help in personal and professional growth
  • To resolve conflicts and maintain a healthy work environment
  • To improve patient satisfaction and outcomes

(d) Barriers to interpersonal relationship (2 marks)

1. Communication barriers

  • Language differences, medical jargon, unclear or conflicting messages, noise, interruptions and poor listening

2. Psychological (emotional) barriers

  • Anxiety, fear, anger, depression, low self-esteem and defensiveness

3. Attitudinal barriers

  • Prejudice, stereotypes, ego, superiority, judgemental attitude, lack of empathy

4. Cultural barriers

  • Differences in values, beliefs, customs, gender roles and ideas about illness

5. Lack of trust

  • Broken promises, inconsistency, breach of confidentiality

6. Organisational barriers

  • Heavy workload, staff shortage, lack of time, rigid hierarchy and poor team meetings

7. Physical barriers

  • Distance, poor environment, hearing and speech problems, unconscious state of the patient

8. Personal barriers

  • Shyness, aggressiveness, poor social skills and lack of self-awareness

(e) Strategies to overcome the barriers (2 marks)

  1. Active listening – give full attention, maintain eye contact, nod, paraphrase and avoid interrupting
  2. Use clear, simple language; avoid jargon; use an interpreter when needed
  3. Show empathy and respect; accept the person without judging
  4. Build trust – be honest, consistent and punctual, keep promises and maintain confidentiality
  5. Use appropriate non-verbal communication – warm facial expression, open posture, appropriate touch
  6. Develop cultural sensitivity – respect beliefs, food and religious practices
  7. Control emotions and use assertive (not aggressive) communication
  8. Give and seek feedback to confirm understanding
  9. Use conflict-resolution skills – discuss the problem, not the person; find win–win solutions
  10. Practise self-awareness – recognise one's own prejudices and moods (the Johari window helps)
  11. Spend time with patients; sit down while talking
  12. Organisational measures – adequate staffing, regular team meetings, clear roles and a culture of mutual respect
  13. Use aids – hearing aids, writing boards, pictures – for patients with communication difficulties

Importance in nursing

  • Good IPR improves patient cooperation, reduces anxiety and complaints, prevents errors through clear teamwork, and increases the nurse's own job satisfaction

Conclusion Interpersonal relationship is a close association built on communication, trust and respect. It may be personal, professional or social; its purposes include meeting needs, giving therapeutic help and promoting teamwork. By recognising barriers and using strategies such as active listening, empathy, trust-building and cultural sensitivity, nurses develop effective therapeutic relationships.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define soft skills. Explain the types of soft skills and their application in nursing. (2 + 5 + 3)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Soft skills are the personal attributes, social abilities and communication skills that enable a person to interact effectively and harmoniously with others
  • They are also called "people skills", "life skills" or "employability skills"
  • They are linked with emotional intelligence and personality, unlike hard skills, which are technical and job-specific
  • Examples: communication, listening, empathy, teamwork, leadership, time management, problem-solving, adaptability and a positive attitude

(b) Types of soft skills (5 marks)

1. Visual skills

  • The ability to send and receive messages through sight – what we see and what others see in us
  • Body language – posture, gestures, facial expression, eye contact, distance (proxemics)
  • Personal appearance and grooming – a neat uniform conveys competence and respect
  • Observation skills – noticing a patient's restlessness, pallor or facial grimace of pain
  • Visual aids – charts, posters, models and pictures used in patient teaching
  • Written communication – legible records, clear notices and reports

2. Aural (listening) skills

  • The ability to listen and understand spoken messages
  • Hearing is a physical process; listening is an active mental process of attending, understanding and responding
  • Active listening – full attention, eye contact, nodding, not interrupting, paraphrasing ("You are worried about the operation…"), asking clarifying questions
  • Listening to tone – recognising worry, anger or pain in the voice
  • Barriers – noise, prejudice, day-dreaming, preparing one's reply while the other is speaking

3. Communication skills

  • Verbal – clear, polite, simple speech; correct pronunciation; appropriate tone and speed
  • Non-verbal – matching body language with words
  • Written – documentation, reports, letters, emails
  • Presentation – health talks, case presentations
  • Therapeutic communication techniques – open-ended questions, reflection, silence, clarification, summarising
  • Telephone and electronic etiquette

4. Interpersonal and relationship-building skills

  • Building rapport with patients, families and the community; empathy; respect; cultural sensitivity

5. Teamwork and collaboration

  • Cooperating with doctors, colleagues and support staff; sharing work; respecting roles

6. Leadership and decision-making

  • Guiding others, taking responsibility, making timely decisions in emergencies

7. Problem-solving and critical thinking

  • Analysing situations and finding practical solutions

8. Time management and organisation

  • Planning, prioritising and completing work on time

9. Emotional intelligence and stress management

  • Self-awareness, self-control, motivation, empathy and social skills (Goleman); coping with stress

10. Adaptability, conflict management and work ethic

  • Accepting change, resolving disagreements calmly, being punctual, honest and responsible

Summary

Type Main components
Visual body language, appearance, observation, visual aids, writing
Aural hearing, active listening, understanding tone
Communication verbal, non-verbal, written, presentation, therapeutic techniques
Others teamwork, leadership, problem-solving, time management, emotional intelligence, adaptability

(c) Application of soft skills in nursing (3 marks)

  • Admission and assessment – greeting the patient warmly, introducing oneself and listening carefully gives a complete and accurate history
  • Therapeutic communication – reduces anxiety before surgery and builds trust
  • Patient education – explaining in simple language with pictures and demonstrations improves understanding and compliance
  • Breaking bad news and end-of-life care – sensitivity, empathy and silence
  • Teamwork – clear handover (e.g. the SBAR format – situation, background, assessment, recommendation) prevents errors
  • Conflict management – calming angry relatives and resolving disagreements among staff
  • Leadership and time management – managing the ward, prioritising care and delegating
  • Cultural competence – respecting the beliefs and practices of patients from different backgrounds
  • Community work – building relationships with community leaders, ASHAs and families for health programmes
  • Self-care – stress management and resilience prevent burnout

Conclusion Soft skills are the personal and interpersonal abilities that make a nurse effective with people. Visual, aural and communication skills, along with teamwork, leadership, time management and emotional intelligence, are applied in every area of nursing – from admission to discharge and from the hospital to the community.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Differentiate between empathy and sympathy.
answer_html:
Introduction Both are responses to another person's feelings, but empathy is therapeutic while sympathy may not be.

Empathy Sympathy
understanding and sharing another's feelings from his point of view – "putting oneself in the other's shoes" feeling pity or sorrow for another's misfortune
the nurse stays objective and emotionally balanced the nurse becomes emotionally involved and may be overwhelmed
helps the patient cope and become independent may make the patient feel pitied and dependent
e.g. "It must be frightening to wait for the report. What worries you most?" e.g. "Oh, poor you – I feel so sad for you."

Nursing: nurses should show empathy, not sympathy – empathy is a core condition of a helping relationship (Carl Rogers).

subject: Applied Psychology
question: What is burnout? List its signs.
answer_html:
Definition Burnout is a state of physical, emotional and mental exhaustion resulting from prolonged work-related stress that has not been successfully managed. WHO (ICD-11) describes it as an occupational phenomenon with three features:

  1. Exhaustion – feeling drained of energy
  2. Mental distance from the job – cynicism and detachment
  3. Reduced professional efficacy

Signs

  • Constant tiredness, sleep problems, headaches, frequent illness
  • Irritability, loss of interest and motivation
  • Detachment from patients, treating them like objects
  • Absenteeism, lateness, more mistakes
  • Feelings of failure; use of alcohol or tobacco to cope

Prevention: adequate staffing and rest, fair duty rotation, peer support and debriefing, exercise, hobbies, counselling.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain assertiveness – its meaning, techniques and importance in nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Assertiveness is the ability to express one's thoughts, feelings, needs and rights honestly, directly and confidently, while respecting the rights and feelings of others. It is the healthy middle path between passive and aggressive behaviour.

A. Passive, aggressive and assertive behaviour

Passive Aggressive Assertive
gives in, hides own needs dominates, blames, shouts honest, firm and respectful
avoids conflict violates others' rights respects both self and others
"Whatever you say…" "You always make mistakes!" "I feel… when… I would like…"
leads to resentment and stress leads to conflict and fear leads to mutual respect

B. Features of assertive behaviour

  • Direct eye contact, upright posture, calm and firm voice
  • Clear, specific message; listens to the other person
  • Can say "no" politely without guilt; accepts and gives feedback

C. Techniques

  1. "I" statements – "I feel concerned when the drug chart is left unsigned, because it can cause errors; I would like us to sign immediately"
  2. Broken record – calmly repeating the request until it is heard
  3. Fogging – calmly agreeing with any part of a criticism that is true, without getting defensive
  4. Negative assertion – accepting genuine mistakes; negative inquiry – asking for specific feedback
  5. Saying no politely and firmly
  6. Workable compromise
  7. DESC script – Describe the situation, Express feelings, Specify what is wanted, state the Consequences
  8. Matching body language with words

D. Importance in nursing

  • Patient advocacy and safety – questioning unclear or unsafe orders; speaking up about risks
  • Clear communication with doctors, colleagues and relatives
  • Handling aggressive relatives, bullying and harassment
  • Delegation and leadership
  • Reduces stress, increases self-esteem and job satisfaction; prevents burnout
  • Teaching patients to be assertive – refusing alcohol or tobacco, asking questions about their treatment

E. Barriers

  • Fear of conflict or punishment, rigid hierarchy
  • Cultural expectations that women should be submissive
  • Low self-esteem and lack of training

F. Example – an assertive response in the ward

  • A relative insists on staying in the room during a dressing
  • Passive: lets him stay, against the rule
  • Aggressive: "Get out! Can't you follow simple rules?"
  • Assertive: "I understand you want to be with your father. The dressing will take about fifteen minutes, and it must be done in a clean area. Please wait outside – I will call you as soon as it is over."

Conclusion Assertiveness is honest, confident and respectful expression of one's views; using techniques such as "I" statements and the DESC script, nurses can advocate for patients, communicate clearly and protect their own wellbeing.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain teamwork – the characteristics of an effective team and its importance in nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction A team is a small group of people with complementary skills who are committed to a common purpose and hold themselves mutually accountable (Katzenbach and Smith). Teamwork is their combined effort to achieve that purpose. The health care team includes doctors, nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists, dietitians, social workers, laboratory and support staff – and the patient and family.

A. Characteristics of an effective team

  1. A clear common goal – the patient's welfare
  2. Clear roles and responsibilities
  3. Open, effective communication – structured handover (e.g. SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation)
  4. Mutual trust and respect
  5. Cooperation and coordination
  6. Shared decision-making and accountability
  7. Good leadership
  8. Constructive conflict resolution
  9. A supportive atmosphere with recognition of good work
  10. Regular evaluation and feedback (debriefing)

B. Stages of team development (Tuckman)

  1. Forming – members meet, roles are unclear
  2. Storming – disagreements and conflicts arise
  3. Norming – rules and roles are agreed; cooperation grows
  4. Performing – the team works efficiently towards its goal
  5. Adjourning – the team ends after the task is complete

C. Importance in nursing

  • Continuity and quality of care; holistic care from many disciplines
  • Patient safety – fewer errors through clear handover and checklists (e.g. the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist)
  • Quick, coordinated response in emergencies (cardiac arrest teams)
  • Efficient use of time and resources
  • Job satisfaction, mutual learning, less stress and burnout
  • Better patient outcomes and satisfaction

D. Barriers to teamwork

  • Poor communication; rigid hierarchy
  • Unclear roles; ego clashes and lack of trust
  • Heavy workload, staff shortage and frequent shift changes

E. The nurse as a good team member

  • Be punctual, reliable and responsible
  • Share information clearly and on time; give complete handovers
  • Help colleagues and respect every member's role
  • Accept feedback and resolve conflicts constructively
  • Follow agreed protocols and policies

F. Example of a structured handover (SBAR)

  • Situation – "Mr Patil in bed 4 has a BP of 90/60 and a pulse of 110."
  • Background – "He is on the first day after hernia repair."
  • Assessment – "I think he may be bleeding; the dressing is soaked."
  • Recommendation – "Please see him now; shall I start the IV fluid as per protocol?"
  • SBAR gives clear, complete information quickly and reduces misunderstanding

Conclusion Teamwork is the coordinated effort of a group with a common goal; effective teams have clear roles, open communication, trust, leadership and feedback, and in nursing they ensure safe, continuous, high-quality patient care.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: List the dimensions of self-empowerment.
answer_html:
Introduction Self-empowerment is taking control of one's own life by making positive choices and developing the confidence and skills to act on them.

Dimensions (psychological empowerment)

  1. Meaning – a sense of purpose; the work matters to the person
  2. Competence (self-efficacy) – belief in one's ability to do the task well
  3. Self-determination (autonomy) – freedom to make choices and decisions
  4. Impact – the feeling that one's actions make a difference

Areas of self-empowerment

  • Physical, emotional, intellectual, social, economic and spiritual

Key qualities: self-awareness, self-esteem, self-confidence, self-reliance and self-discipline.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Enumerate the elements of personal grooming for a nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Personal grooming means keeping oneself clean, neat and presentable. A well-groomed nurse inspires confidence and helps prevent infection.

Elements of personal grooming

  1. Personal hygiene – daily bath, clean body, use of deodorant
  2. Clean, ironed uniform of the correct size, with name badge
  3. Hair – neatly tied or pinned up, off the collar, covered with a cap where required
  4. Nails – short, clean, without nail polish or artificial nails
  5. Minimal jewellery – no rings, bangles or dangling earrings in clinical areas
  6. Oral hygiene – fresh breath
  7. Clean, comfortable, closed footwear that makes no noise
  8. Light make-up and no strong perfume
  9. Good posture and a pleasant facial expression

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the importance of women's empowerment in society.
answer_html:
Introduction Women's empowerment is the process of increasing women's ability to make choices and control their own lives – through education, health, economic independence, legal rights and participation in decision-making. Gender equality is also one of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG 5). An empowered woman benefits not only herself but her whole family and society.

Importance of women's empowerment

1. Better health of women and children

  • Empowered women make decisions about their own health, nutrition, birth spacing and institutional delivery
  • This lowers maternal mortality, infant mortality and malnutrition

2. Education of the family

  • "Educate a woman and you educate a family" – educated mothers ensure schooling, immunisation and hygiene for their children

3. Economic development

  • Women's participation in the workforce increases family income and national productivity; it reduces poverty
  • Self-help groups and micro-credit have helped many rural women start small businesses

4. Reduction of social evils

  • Helps fight dowry, child marriage, female foeticide, domestic violence and trafficking

5. Control over family size

  • Empowered women tend to marry later and have fewer, healthier children

6. Political participation and decision-making

  • One-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities are reserved for women (73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments)
  • The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (2023) provides for one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies, to come into force after the next census and delimitation

7. Gender equality and human rights

  • Equal rights to education, property, employment and safety

8. Social development and role models

  • Empowered women become leaders and role models for the next generation of girls

Government initiatives in India

  • Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana, Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana, One Stop Centres (Sakhi), Women Helpline 181, Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 (26 weeks' paid maternity leave), and self-help groups under the National Rural Livelihood Mission

Role of the nurse

  • Health education on nutrition, family planning and safe motherhood
  • Encouraging girls' education and preventing early marriage
  • Informing women about schemes, legal rights and helplines
  • Identifying and supporting victims of domestic violence
  • Being a role model – nursing itself is a profession that has empowered many women

Conclusion Women's empowerment improves health, education, income and social justice; it is essential for the development of the family, the community and the nation, and nurses play an active part in promoting it.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Describe professional etiquette for nurses.
answer_html:
Introduction Professional etiquette is the code of polite, respectful and appropriate behaviour expected of a person in a profession. For nurses, good etiquette builds the trust of patients and colleagues and reflects the dignity of the nursing profession.

1. Personal appearance and grooming

  • Clean, ironed uniform with name badge; hair neatly tied; short nails without polish; minimal jewellery; closed, quiet footwear; personal and oral hygiene; no strong perfume

2. Punctuality and discipline

  • Report on time, complete the handover and do not leave duty without proper relief

3. Courtesy towards patients

  • Greet patients, introduce yourself and address them respectfully ("Mr. Patil", "Aaji", "Kaka"), never by bed number or diagnosis
  • Knock before entering, maintain privacy, and explain before every procedure
  • Treat every patient equally irrespective of caste, religion, gender or economic status

4. Confidentiality

  • Do not discuss patients in corridors, lifts, canteens or on social media
  • Never photograph patients or post hospital matters online

5. Communication etiquette

  • Speak politely in a calm tone; avoid shouting, gossip and arguments in front of patients
  • Telephone etiquette – answer promptly, identify yourself and the ward, take messages accurately
  • Avoid personal mobile phone use during duty
  • Write professional, clear notes and emails

6. Relations with colleagues and seniors

  • Respect the hierarchy and the roles of others; cooperate and share work
  • Give and accept constructive feedback privately
  • Do not criticise colleagues in front of patients

7. Honesty and accountability

  • Report errors promptly; admit mistakes; do not falsify records

8. Professional boundaries

  • Be caring without over-involvement; do not accept money or expensive gifts; avoid personal relationships with patients

9. Cultural sensitivity

  • Respect patients' religious practices, dietary customs and modesty

10. Conduct outside the hospital

  • Behave in a way that does not bring disrepute to the profession; follow the code of ethics of the Indian Nursing Council

Conclusion Professional etiquette – neat appearance, punctuality, courtesy, confidentiality, respectful communication, teamwork and honesty – helps nurses earn trust and uphold the dignity of nursing.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define self-empowerment. Explain its dimensions, the ways of developing self-empowerment and the role of the nurse in empowering others. (2 + 3 + 3 + 2)

diagram.caption: Johari window – open, blind, hidden and unknown areas of the self

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Empowerment means giving power, authority or ability to someone
  • Self-empowerment is the process of taking control of one's own life – recognising one's strengths, making positive choices, setting goals and developing the confidence, knowledge and skills to achieve them
  • An empowered person believes "I can", takes responsibility for his decisions and does not depend on others for every choice
  • Features: self-awareness, self-confidence, self-reliance, responsibility, positive attitude and continuous learning

(b) Dimensions of self-empowerment (3 marks)

A. Psychological dimensions (Spreitzer)

  1. Meaning – the person values his work and goals; there is a fit between his beliefs and what he does
  2. Competence (self-efficacy) – the belief in one's ability to perform tasks well (Albert Bandura's concept of self-efficacy)
  3. Self-determination (autonomy) – the freedom to choose how to act and to make one's own decisions
  4. Impact – the belief that one's actions make a difference at work and in society

B. Areas (domains) of self-empowerment

  1. Physical – caring for one's own health, fitness and safety
  2. Emotional – recognising and managing feelings; emotional resilience
  3. Intellectual – knowledge, skills, critical thinking and continuous learning
  4. Social – healthy relationships, assertiveness, the ability to ask for help and to help others
  5. Economic – financial independence and the ability to manage money
  6. Spiritual – values, purpose and inner peace

C. Core personal qualities

  • Self-awareness, self-esteem, self-confidence, self-motivation, self-discipline and self-reliance

(c) Ways of developing self-empowerment (3 marks)

  1. Develop self-awareness
    • Know your strengths, weaknesses, values and feelings; use a personal SWOT analysis (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats)
    • The Johari window helps: seek feedback to reduce the blind area and share appropriately to enlarge the open area
  2. Set clear, realistic goals – use SMART goals and break them into small steps
  3. Build knowledge and skills – continuing education, workshops, reading, learning computers and languages
  4. Build self-esteem – positive self-talk, recognise achievements, stop comparing with others
  5. Be assertive – express needs and opinions honestly and respectfully; learn to say "no"
  6. Take responsibility for decisions and actions instead of blaming others or circumstances
  7. Develop decision-making and problem-solving skills
  8. Manage time and stress – plan, prioritise, relax
  9. Maintain a healthy lifestyle – exercise, nutrition, sleep
  10. Build a support network – mentors, role models, supportive friends and family
  11. Learn from failures – treat mistakes as lessons; persist
  12. Achieve financial independence – savings and wise spending

Barriers to self-empowerment: low self-esteem, fear of failure, dependency on others, lack of education and information, gender discrimination, cultural restrictions and lack of opportunities.

(d) Role of the nurse in empowering others (2 marks)

1. Empowering patients

  • Give complete, understandable information about illness and treatment so that patients can make informed decisions and give informed consent
  • Respect autonomy – involve patients in planning their care
  • Teach self-care skills – insulin injection, blood sugar monitoring, stoma care, breast self-examination
  • Encourage independence in activities of daily living, especially in rehabilitation and the elderly

2. Empowering families

  • Train family caregivers in home care, and inform them about support services

3. Empowering the community

  • Health education, mothers' meetings, adolescent groups and self-help groups
  • Training and supporting ASHAs and anganwadi workers
  • Promoting women's health, girls' education and awareness of rights and schemes

4. Empowering colleagues and students

  • Mentoring, appropriate delegation with authority, recognising good work, encouraging continuing education and participation in decisions (shared governance)

5. Advocacy

  • Speak up for patients' rights, dignity and safety, especially for vulnerable groups

Conclusion Self-empowerment is taking control of one's own life through self-awareness, goals, skills and confidence. It has psychological dimensions – meaning, competence, self-determination and impact – and physical, emotional, intellectual, social, economic and spiritual areas. An empowered nurse, in turn, empowers patients, families, colleagues and the community.

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Define gender discrimination. Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition Gender discrimination is the unequal or unfair treatment of a person because of his or her gender, which denies equal rights and opportunities. In India it mostly affects women and girls, and also transgender persons.

Examples

  1. Son preference, female foeticide and infanticide – the child sex ratio was 919 girls per 1,000 boys (Census 2011)
  2. Less education for girls; early marriage
  3. Less nutritious food and health care for girls and women
  4. Unequal wages, fewer jobs and promotions; unpaid household work
  5. Dowry and domestic violence
  6. Limited property rights and say in decisions
  7. Sexual harassment at the workplace

Legal safeguards: the Constitution forbids discrimination by sex (Articles 14, 15, 16); the PCPNDT Act (against sex selection) and the POSH Act, 2013 (against workplace sexual harassment).

subject: Applied Psychology
question: Explain the barriers to women's empowerment in India.
answer_html:
Introduction Women's empowerment is the process by which women gain power and control over their own lives – through education, health, economic independence, decision-making and equal rights. Despite progress, many barriers remain in India.

1. Social and cultural barriers

  • Patriarchy and gender stereotypes – women seen mainly as homemakers
  • Son preference; restrictions on women's mobility and dress
  • Child marriage – about one in four women aged 20–24 were married before 18 (NFHS-5)
  • Dowry and the low value given to girls

2. Educational barriers

  • Lower female literacy than male literacy
  • Girls drop out of school because of household work, distance, safety concerns and lack of toilets or menstrual facilities

3. Economic barriers

  • Low participation of women in paid work; much unpaid domestic and care work
  • Wage gap; few women own land or property
  • Limited access to credit, skills training and markets

4. Health barriers

  • Anaemia affects more than half of Indian women (NFHS-5)
  • Malnutrition, maternal deaths and poor access to reproductive health care
  • Little control over decisions about pregnancy and family planning

5. Violence and insecurity

  • Domestic violence, dowry harassment, sexual harassment and trafficking
  • Fear for safety restricts education, work and travel

6. Political barriers

  • Low representation in Parliament and state assemblies; the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (2023) provides one-third reservation, to be implemented after delimitation
  • Women panchayat members sometimes act as proxies for male relatives

7. Legal barriers

  • Lack of awareness of rights and laws; slow justice; social pressure not to complain

8. Psychological barriers

  • Low self-esteem and lack of confidence; conditioning to accept a subordinate role; dependence on male family members

9. Digital divide

  • Fewer women own mobile phones or use the internet, limiting access to information and services

10. Double burden

  • Balancing work and family without childcare support or family help

Overcoming the barriers

  • Education of girls; scholarships and safe transport
  • Self-help groups, microfinance and skill development
  • Legal literacy and strict enforcement of laws
  • Gender sensitisation of men and boys
  • Better health and nutrition services; political participation

Role of the nurse

  • Health education of women and girls – nutrition, anaemia, menstrual and reproductive health
  • Empower women patients to take part in decisions about their own health
  • Identify and support victims of violence
  • Be a role model of an educated, independent working woman

Conclusion Women's empowerment in India is held back by social, educational, economic, health, safety, political, legal and psychological barriers; education, economic independence, legal protection and changing attitudes – supported by nurses – can overcome them.
